case_name: 604598 Saskatchewan Ltd. (c.o.b. Great Canadian Superbar) v. Saskatchewan (Liquor and Gaming Authority)
text:
Dated:

THE COURT OF APPEAL FOR SASKATCHEWAN

THE SASKATCHEWAN
LIQUOR AND GAMING AUTHORITY

APPELLANT

- and -

604598
SASKATCHEWAN LTD. carrying on business under the name of "THE GREAT
CANADIAN SUPERBAR "

RESPONDENT

-and-

THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
FOR SASKATCHEWAN

INTERESTED PARTY

CORAM:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Cameron

The Honourable Mr. Justice Lane

The Honourable Madam Justice Jackson

COUNSEL:

Mr. D. Kovatch for the Liquor and Gaming Authority

Ms. S. Folkins for the Attorney General

Mr. R. Dumonceaux for the respondent

Mr. P. Koskie for the Liquor and Gaming Licensing
Commission

DISPOSITION:

Appeal Heard:                May 8 and 9, 1997

Appeal Decided:             February 5, 1998

On Appeal From:           QB 2226/96 J.C. Saskatoon

Appeal File:                   No. 2670

Reasons by:                   (1) The Honourable Madam
Justice Jackson

(2) The Honourable Mr. Justice Lane

(3) The Honourable Mr. Justice Cameron

JACKSON J.A.

Summary

[
1
]    This appeal falls to be determined principally on the question of
standing to challenge the constitutional validity of s. 54(1)(b) of the
Alcohol
Control Regulations
, 1994, c. A-18.01 Reg.3. (Legal standing is explained
by Thomas A. Cromwell in
Locus Standi: A Commentary on the Law of Standing
in Canada,
p. 7 as the entitlement to seek judicial relief apart from
questions of the substantive merits.)  Superbar is not entitled to standing as
of right or to standing in the public interest to argue that s.54(1)(b)
contravenes s. 2(b) of the
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

[
2
]    Standing as of right is afforded to those individuals or
corporations who are exceptionally prejudiced by a law.  Superbar is denied
standing as of right because the impugned regulation does not affect Superbar
differently than any other holder of a liquor license.  The regulation does not
prohibit exotic dancing absolutely.  It only prohibits exotic dancing where
liquor is sold.  Superbar can thus offer exotic dancing if it chooses---to the
extent not prohibited by the
Criminal Code
---as can anyone else in
Saskatchewan.  Superbar just cannot offer liquor and exotic dancing in the same
premises at the same time.  But then neither can anyone else.  Moreover, recent
case authority from the Supreme Court of Canada indicates that the fact
Superbar faces a suspension for contravening the regulation does not justify a
grant of standing as of right.

[
3
]     A court has a discretion to grant standing if it is in the public
interest to do so.  Before a court can exercise its discretion to grant public
interest standing (i) there must be a serious issue as to the law’s validity,
(ii) the applicant must be directly affected by the Act or have a genuine
interest in its validity, and (iii) there must be no other reasonable and
effective way to test the law’s validity.  Superbar has not satisfied the Court
it meets the third criterion.  Based on the evidence, there is someone better
able to assert a challenge to this regulation: the dancers themselves.
Granting public interest standing to Superbar to argue that this law infringes
the freedom of expression of the dancers when there is no evidence from them or
from a surrogate could lead to a questionable result based on incomplete
evidence. Insofar as Superbar asserts that s. 54(1)(b) offends s. 2(b) on the
footing that any prohibition against striptease performances is
unconstitutional, again, we have no evidence addressed to this issue.

[
4
]    If standing were to be granted, the appeal would have to be
allowed in any event, as there is no evidence directed to the meaning and
content of striptease dancing or its effects--all this is necessary evidence to
determine if s. 2(b) is infringed.  Accordingly, I would allow the appeal and restore
the suspension imposed by the Commission.

Issues

[
5
]    The broad threshold issues are: (i) Does Superbar have standing to
challenge the constitutional validity of s. 54(1)(b) of
The Alcohol Control
Regulations, 1994
? (ii) If Superbar does have standing, can it make the
constitutional argument given the evidentiary base before the Court?  As will
become evident, there is a link between these two issues.  This application
proceeded on the basis that s. 54(1)(b) concerned subject matter that was
placed beyond the legislative and executive power of the legislature by
s. 2(b)

of the
Charter
, but the activities of specific dancers, including the
Men of Extreme, were used as an example---and the only example---of the type of
activity constrained by the regulation’s prohibition against strip tease
performances.

Procedural
History

[
6
]    These proceedings began with the Liquor and Gaming Authority’s
letter of May 21, 1996 to Superbar advising of a five-day suspension of its
“Restaurant Permit with Lounge Endorsement.”  The Authority advised that one
reason for the suspension was that “several male strippers had performed in
contravention of s. 54(1)(b)” on three nights during the spring of 1996.

Section 54(1)(b)
of the
Regulations
provides:

54(1) It is a term and condition of every permit that
no permittee shall permit or allow in the permitted premises:

...

(b) any activity or entertainment that consists of a
striptease performance or wet clothing contest.

Exercising its
right of review under
s. 18
of
The
Alcohol and Gaming Regulation Act
,
S.S. 1988-89, c. A-18.01, Superbar asked the Liquor and Gaming Commission to
review the Authority’s decision
.
Superbar requested a review on the
basis that it had not allowed any activity that consisted of a striptease
performance.

[
7
]    At the review hearing before the Commission, the Authority led
evidence from two inspectors and a competitor who had observed men removing
items of clothing while dancing.  Superbar gave its evidence through its owner
and manager who sought to persuade the Commission that Superbar had not offered
a striptease performance as the men removed only some and not all of their
clothing.  The chambers judge fairly and accurately summarized all this
evidence in paras. [9] to [26] of his decision which are contained in Appendix
“A” to these reasons.

[
8
]    In a letter reproduced in the chamber judge’s decision, the
Commission upheld the Authority’s decision to suspend Superbar’s liquor
permit.  The Commission gave few reasons.  They  “strongly based their decision
on s. 54(1)(b) of the regulations” and they also said Superbar had “displayed a
disregard for the spirit and intent of the rules.”

[
9
]    Superbar applied to quash the Commission’s decision on the basis
that the principles of natural justice had not been followed.  Superbar also
said the Commission had exceeded its jurisdiction by determining that a breach
of the “spirit and intent of the rules” was sufficient to ground a suspension.
The application was supported by an affidavit sworn by Superbar’s owner
speaking only to the fairness of the hearing.

[
10
]   Some time later, Superbar served notice pursuant to
The

Constitutional Questions Act
R.S.S. 1978, c. C-29 asking the Queen’s Bench
for---among other matters which were not argued on this appeal---(i) an order
quashing the Commission’s decision on the basis that s. 54(1)(b) of the
regulations contravened s. 2(b); or (ii)  a declaration that s. 54(1)(b) is
inconsistent with the
Charter
and is therefore of no force and effect.

[
11
]   No other evidence was filed to support this new aspect of the
proceedings.  The Attorney General for Saskatchewan did not appear in the
Queen’s Bench or file any evidence on the motion.  His counsel advised this
Court they did not do so because it was believed the standing issue would carry
the day.  Given this, the Crown sought---before this Court---to adduce evidence
under
s. 1
of the
Charter

to show why this regulation, if found to be
unconstitutional, could be justified in a free and democratic society.  Even
though most of this new evidence could be described as relating to legislative
facts, Superbar did not consent to the Court considering it.  Indeed, Superbar
resisted the Court’s consideration of this material so strenuously that counsel
withdrew her request that the Court do so.

[
12
]   Thus this case---to determine whether s. 54(1)(b) contravenes s.
2(b) of the
Charter
---is to be determined solely on the evidence before
the Commission which did not include the testimony of the dancers or any patrons
or any broad-based evidence as to the meaning and purpose of the regulation
beyond the evidence of what someone else said the dancers did.  Indeed, freedom
of expression was not the issue addressed by the evidence led before the
Commission.

[
13
]   With this by way of procedural background we turn to the law of
standing.

Law of Standing

[
14
]   The usual starting point for a discussion of standing is
Smith
v. Attorney General of Ontario,

1924 CanLII 3 (SCC)
,
[1924] S.C.R. 331
. Mr. Smith, an Ontario
resident, tried to order a case of whiskey from a retailer who refused to fill
the order because the
Canada Temperance Act
prohibited such activity.
When Mr. Smith sought to challenge the constitutionality of that
Act
,
Duff J. said (at p.337):

...that to accede to appellant’s contention upon this
point would involve the consequence that virtually every resident of Ontario
could maintain a similar action; and we can discover no firm ground on which
the appellant’s claim can be supported which would not be equally available to
sustain the right of any citizen of a province to initiate proceedings
impeaching the constitutional validity of any legislation directly affecting
him, along with other citizens, in a similar way in his business or in his
personal life.

Duff J. formulated
the general rule on standing as of right (at p. 337):

An individual, for example, has no status to maintain
an action restraining a wrongful violation of a public right unless he is
exceptionally prejudiced by the wrongful act.

Three
significant cases have modernized this area of the law:
Thorson v. Attorney
General of Canada
,
1974 CanLII 6 (SCC)
,
[1975] 1 S.C.R. 138
,
Nova Scotia Board of Censors v.
McNeil,
1975 CanLII 14 (SCC)
,
[1976] 2 S.C.R. 265
,
Minister of Justice of Canada v. Borowski
,

1981 CanLII 34 (SCC)
,
[1981] 2 S.C.R. 575
.  Prior to
Thorson
, a litigant seeking to argue a
law’s constitutionality had to demonstrate some interference with a private
right or special damage peculiar to oneself.  (Le Dain J. provides a
comprehensive summary of the prior law, its theory and rationale in
Finlay
v. Canada (Minister of Finance)

1986 CanLII 6 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C. R. 607
.)

[
15
]
Thorson, McNeil
and
Borowski
added a new dimension to

Smith
by permitting a Court to grant standing in the public interest and
as a matter of discretion to a litigant who could not claim standing as of
right.  Although there is some debate about the extent of the new rules
generated by each case in the trilogy, Martland J.’s words
in
Borowski

are most often cited as summarizing the thrust of the new approach to standing
(at p. 598):

I interpret these cases as deciding that to establish
status as a plaintiff in a suit seeking a declaration that legislation is
invalid, if there is a serious issue as to its invalidity, a person need only
to show that he is affected by it directly or that he has a genuine interest as
a citizen in the validity of the legislation and that there is no other
reasonable and effective manner in which the issue may be brought before the
Court.

[
16
]   Since the trilogy and to distinguish public interest standing from
the general rule of standing laid down
in
Smith
,
the latter is sometimes
referred to as “standing” as of right or private interest standing.  I use both
of these phrases in this judgment.

[
17
]   The Supreme Court of Canada has had occasion to further refine and
clarify the standing law in
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.

1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
[1985] 1 S.C.R.
295
,
Finlay, supra,

Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec
,
1989 CanLII 87 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R.
927
,
R. v. Wholesale Travel Group Inc.,
1991 CanLII 39 (SCC)
,
[1991] 3 S.C.R. 154
,
Canadian
Council of Churches v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration),

1992 CanLII 116 (SCC)
,
[1992] 1 S.C.R. 236
and
Hy and Zel.’s Inc. Ontario (Attorney General)
1993 CanLII 30 (SCC)
,
[1993]
3 S.C.R. 675
.

[
18
]   Two issues relevant to this appeal remain: (i) the effect of the
trilogy on private interest standing; and (ii) the extent to which the
evidentiary base affects the decision to grant or withhold standing.  Both
these issues are raised by this appeal.

Effect of
Public Interest Standing on Standing as of Right

[
19
]   What remains of standing as of right after the trilogy?  The
trilogy’s effect on standing as of right is particularly relevant since the
advent of the
Charter
which expands the courts’ power to ensure the
constitutionality of laws.  Whenever anyone seeks to set aside a law as
unconstitutional, the factors
mentioned in
Borowski
--- (i) serious
issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) no other reasonable and effective means of
testing the law---are relevant.  This is so whether one claims “exceptional
prejudice”
in the
Smith
sense or asserts standing as a public interest
litigant.
Finlay
illustrates this point.

[
20
]   Mr. Finlay, a social assistance recipient, sought a declaration
that payments by the federal government to the province of Manitoba were
illegal, on the ground that Manitoba was not fulfilling its obligations under a
federal-provincial cost-sharing agreement.  In particular, Mr. Finlay was
concerned that a deduction from his monthly allowance to recover a prior
overpayment contravened Manitoba’s undertaking to provide needy person’s
assistance no lower than the cost of basic requirements.  If the declaration
Mr. Finlay sought were to be granted, it would not change the Manitoba
practice, but Mr. Finlay believed it would be a persuasive factor in
negotiating a result in his favour.

[
21
]   A unanimous Court refused Mr. Finlay standing as of right.  Le Dain
J., speaking for the Court, said Mr. Finlay was not directly affected by the
federal government’s transfer payments to Manitoba.  For him to be directly
affected, the Court had to be certain that Manitoba would change its
legislation to benefit him.  The causal link between the requested declaration
of illegality and Mr. Finlay receiving a personal remedy was “too indirect,
remote or speculative to be a sufficient causative relationship for standing
under the general rule” (at 623 & 624):

There is no doubt that the respondent has a
direct, personal interest in the alleged provincial non-compliance with the
conditions and undertakings imposed by the Plan.  A declaration that the
federal cost-sharing payments are illegal would necessarily involve a finding
that a province had failed to comply with the conditions and undertakings
imposed by the Plan, but this would not affect the validity of the provincial
legislative provisions about which complaint is made.  Cf.
Re Lofstrom and
Murphy

(1971),
1971 CanLII 936 (SK CA)
,
22 D.L.R. (3d) 120 (Sask. C.A.)
See also
Leblanc v. City
of Transcona
,
1973 CanLII 174 (SCC)
,
[1974] S.C.R.  1261
,
per
Spence J. at p. 1268.  It
cannot be asserted for a certainty that the province would feel compelled by
such a finding to change the offending legislative provisions.  The effect on
provincial action of a declaration that the federal payments are illegal and
even an injunction to stop them is also necessarily a matter of speculation.

...

Although I have experienced some difficulty
on this question, I am on balance of the view that the relationship between the
prejudice allegedly caused to the respondent by the provincial non-compliance
with the conditions and undertakings imposed by the Plan and the alleged
illegality of the federal payments is too indirect, remote or speculative to be
a sufficient causative relationship for standing under the general rule.  The
respondent must therefore in my opinion rely for standing on what is
essentially a public interest in the legality of the federal cost-sharing
payments, albeit that of a particular class of the public defined by the Plan
as persons in need.  It is accordingly necessary to consider whether the
respondent should be recognized as having standing, as a matter of judicial
discretion, by application of the principle or approach reflected in the

decisions of this Court in
Thorson
, McNeil
and
Borowski.

Le Dain J. went on
to find that it would be an appropriate exercise of the Court’s discretion to
grant Mr. Finlay standing as a public interest litigant based on the criteria
laid down
in
Borowski
.

[
22
]   Then, in
Hy and Zel.’s
, a retailer---who had breached a
store closing law---and some of its employees applied for a declaration that
the law under which the retailer had been charged was unconstitutional and,
they too, were refused standing as of right.  The issue was not raised as part
of the prosecution against the retailer, but came to the courts by way of
application.

[
23
]   Major J., speaking for the majority, considered whether the
appellants met the
Borowski

test
for public interest standing.  After
making the assumption that there was a serious question as to the legislation’s
validity, he turned to the question of “direct effect or genuine interest.”  He
concluded that the
Act
clearly had a direct effect on the appellants
because they were all subject to criminal prosecution.

[
24
]   Notwithstanding his conclusion that the
Act
had a direct
effect on the appellants, he refused standing saying they had not met the third
criterion, i.e., they had not demonstrated there were no other reasonable and
effective means of bringing the issue before the courts.  He said this third
criterion “lies at the heart of the discretion to grant public interest
standing” (at p. 692). He noted that the appellants were relying on evidence
filed in another prosecution and said “[t]he very fact that the appellants rely
on the
Peel (Regional Municipality) v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Co. of
Canada
evidence suggests there may be a more reasonable and effective
matter [sic.] of bringing this matter before the court” (at p. 693).  On the
question of standing as of right, Major J. wrote:

In my opinion, this is not the proper case for
deciding the extent to which
Smith
survives in view of the more liberal
views relating to public interest standing.  The appellants have not presented
any evidence as to how they themselves have suffered exceptional prejudice
under the
Smith
test.

[
25
]   L’Heureux-Dubé J. wrote the dissenting judgment in
Hy and Zel.’s

for herself and McLachlin J.  She would have accorded the appellants standing
as of right, but would have also granted them public interest standing.  She
wrote (at pp. 707 & 708):

At this point, the following question must
be addressed, specifically:  should the rules recently developed by this Court
as regards public interest litigants govern those litigants who fall squarely
within
the rule in
Smith
?
In other words, should the trilogy test bar
the standing of those litigants who would otherwise benefit from
the rule in
Smith
?

The question arises because, in this case, while the appellants, of
necessity, also fall into the category of “public interest litigants”, in my
opinion they are better described as persons who experience “exceptional
prejudice” under the Act.  Thus, as I shall outline, the rules for public
interest standing articulated in the trilogy may not be tailored to meet their
particular interests in the present litigation.

The position of the appellants, in contrast
to that of the public interest litigant, may be described as follows.  The
basic thrust of public interest standing is to provide an avenue of access to
the courts to those who, because they have no cause of action under traditional
rules, lack the means of bringing their concerns before the courts.  The
expanded rules of public interest were intended to accommodate such persons so
that legislation would not be otherwise immunized from attack.  However, what
litigants such as the appellants seek is standing to argue the
constitutionality of a law by which they are directly and particularly
affected.

In my view, this general rule of standing
set out
in
Smith
remains applicable to litigants seeking declarations
under the
Charter
as well as in the ordinary case.  There is nothing in
the trilogy to suggest otherwise.  Thus, litigants are still entitled to
standing as long as they are able to establish that they are “exceptionally
prejudiced” by the legislation’s effect on their private rights.  Where such
litigants, in addition, face criminal or quasi-criminal procedures and would be
allowed to raise the constitutionality of the legislation in defence, the
arguments in favour of entitlement to standing seem unassailable.  In the
result, standing is available to such litigants commencing declaratory actions
on the basis of the
Charter.

Later,
L’Heureux-Dubé J. said “...it is difficult to rationalize a rule that permits a
plaintiff to challenge the constitutionality of a law regulating his daily
affairs once he is charged with an offence but not before” (at p. 715).

[
26
]   In making this last point, she is referring to that aspect of standing
law which emanates from
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
Big M Drug Mart was
charged with unlawfully carrying on the sale of goods on a Sunday contrary to
the
Lord’s Day Act
, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, s.4.  It sought to declare the
law unconstitutional on the ground that s. 4 of the
Lord’s Day Act

infringed the right to freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by the
Charter
.
The Crown resisted this argument on the basis that freedom of religion is a
personal freedom and that a corporation, being a statutory creation, cannot be
said to have a conscience or hold a religious belief.  Dickson J., speaking for
the majority, said there could be no question that Big M Drug Mart was entitled
to challenge the validity of the legislation.  He emphasized that:  “[a] law
which itself infringes religious freedom is, by that reason alone, inconsistent
with
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and it matters not whether the accused is a
Christian, Jew, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, atheist, agnostic or whether an
individual or a corporation.  It is the nature of the law, not the status of
the accused, that is in issue” (see p. 314).  He wrote (at pp. 313 & 314):

Section 52 sets out the fundamental principle of
constitutional law that the Constitution is supreme.  The undoubted corollary to
be drawn from this principle is that no one can be convicted of an offence
under an unconstitutional law.  The respondent did not come to court
voluntarily as an interested citizen asking for a prerogative declaration that
a statute is unconstitutional.  If it had been engaged in such “public interest
litigation” it would have had to fulfill the status requirements laid down by
this Court in the trilogy of “standing”
cases (
Thorson v. Attorney General
of Canada
,
1974 CanLII 6 (SCC)
,
[1975] 1 S.C.R. 138
,
Nova Scotia Board of Censors v. McNeil
,
1975 CanLII 14 (SCC)
,
[1976]
2 S.C.R. 265
,
Minister of Justice of Canada v. Borowski
,
1981 CanLII 34 (SCC)
,
[1981] 2 S.C.R.
575
) but that was not the reason for its appearance in Court.

Any accused, whether corporate or individual, may
defend a criminal charge by arguing that the law under which the charge is
brought is constitutionally invalid.  Big M is urging that the law under which
it has been charged is inconsistent with
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and by
reason of
s. 52
of the
Constitution Act, 1982,
it is of no force or
effect.

He expanded this
(at p. 316):

The respondent Big M was commanded by Her Majesty the
Queen to face prosecution for a violation of an Act of Parliament.  It came to
court, not for the purpose of having the Act declared unconstitutional, but in
order to secure a dismissal of the charges against it.  The Provincial Court
Judge was not called upon to make either a prerogative declaration or a s.
24(1) order.  He simply was asked to prevent a violation of the fundamental
principle of constitutional law embodied in s. 52(1) by dismissing the charges.

The law is clearly
stated: an accused, whether corporate or individual, may defend a criminal
charge by arguing that a third party’s rights are infringed under the law.

[
27
]   Thus, standing as of right remains a separate means of gaining
access to the courts with a different threshold and rules than public interest
standing.  An applicant may assert personal exceptional prejudice or, if
charged with a criminal offence,  that a third party’s rights are infringed
unconstitutionally by the law under which the charge is laid.

Relevance of
the Evidentiary Base in Determining Standing

[
28
]   The other issue is linked to the question of deciding the extent to
which a Court can consider the evidence before it in determining whether
standing should be granted.  Many of the cases to which I have referred
considered standing as a preliminary point.  But in this case--as in
Hy and
Zel.’s--
all the applicant’s evidence is before the Court.  As I indicated
above, Major J. referred to the evidentiary base upon which standing was
decided in
Hy and Zel.’s
(at pp. 692 & 693):

Courts are often called upon to determine
standing as a preliminary point.  Indeed, this Court
decided
Thorson
, Nova
Scotia Board of Censors, Finlay,
and
Canadian Council of Churches
as
preliminary matters.  As
stated by Le Dain J. in
Finlay
,
at p. 617, a
court’s ability to consider standing at the outset “depends on the nature of
the issues raised and on whether the court has sufficient material before it,
in the way of allegations of fact, considerations of law, and argument, for a
proper understanding at a preliminary stage of the nature of the interest
asserted.”  Since the appellants’ case has proceeded without trial the
situation is akin to determining standing as a preliminary point.

The appellants allege the Act violates both
freedom of religion and equality rights but have presented almost no original
evidence in support of their claim.  The Magder application relies on the
evidence filed in the Attorney General’s s. 8 application.  The s. 8
application was stayed and never brought on for trial.  In any event, the s. 8
application did not involve any retail employees and would not provide evidence
to establish their standing.  The Hy & Zel’s application relies on the
evidence filed in
Peel (Regional Municipality) v. Great Atlantic &
Pacific Co. of Canada,
with a few additional affidavits.
The very fact
that the appellants rely on the Peel (Regional Municipality v. Great Atlantic
& Pacific Co. of Canada evidence suggests there may be a more reasonable
and effective matter of bringing this matter before the court.
(Emphasis added)

Thus, for the
majority in
Hy and Zel.’s
the evidence demonstrated there was a more
reasonable and effective manner of bringing the matter before the Court and
this resulted in a refusal of public interest standing.

[
29
]   The issue of the appropriate evidentiary base was first raised
in
McNeil
.

Laskin C.J. wrote
(at pp. 267 & 268):

In granting leave, this Court indicated
that where, as here, there is an arguable case for according standing, it is
preferable to have all the issues in the case, whether going to procedural
regularity or propriety or to the merits, decided at the same time.  A
thoroughgoing examination of the challenged statute could have a bearing in
clarifying any disputed question on standing.
I note that in
Smith
v.
Attorney General of Ontario
, Duff J. thought that the issue of standing was
an arguable one and since the merits had been canvassed “we are loath to give a
judgment against the appellant solely based upon a fairly disputable point of
procedure, and accordingly we think it right to say that in our opinion the appellant’s
action also fails in substance” (at p. 338).

Although the merits have not been canvassed
in this case, it has not been disputed by any of the counsel who supported the
position of the appellant, being appellant’s counsel and counsel for the Attorney
General of Ontario, of Alberta and of Saskatchewan, that a serious, a
substantial constitutional issue has been raised by the respondent’s
declaratory proceeding.  The question of standing here begins with this feature
of the proceeding, just as it did
in
Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada
.

[
30
]   The Supreme Court returned to this issue
in
Finlay
.  After
canvassing the authorities, Le Dain J. said (at p. 617):

It depends on the nature of the issues
raised and whether the court has sufficient material before it, in the way of
allegations of fact, considerations of law, and argument, for a proper
understanding at a preliminary stage of the nature of the interest asserted.
In my opinion, the present case is one in which the question of standing can be
properly determined on a motion to strike.  The nature of the respondent’s
interest in the substantive issues raised by his action is sufficiently clearly
established by the allegations and contentions in the statement of claim and
the statutory and contractual provisions relied on without the need of evidence
or full argument on the merits.

[
31
]   From this, I conclude that a court should be cautious about mixing
questions of standing and the sufficiency of the evidence.  It would be
inappropriate for a court to refuse standing in a manner which indicated the
litigant would have standing if he or she had a better evidentiary base. As
Kent Roach says in
Constitutional Remedies in Canada
(at p. 5-22)
“standing should also not be denied because a court has concerns that a claim
is not ripe or factually specific.”  Nonetheless, based on
Hy and Zel.’s,

there is a point where a person will be refused standing because the lack of
evidence demonstrates to the court that there is a more reasonable and
effective manner to challenge the impugned law.

[
32
]   This brings me to the application of the law to the resolution of
three questions: (i) can Superbar assert standing as of right on the basis that
it is exceptionally prejudiced; (ii) can Superbar be brought within the Big M
Drug Mart doctrine; and (iii) can Superbar assert standing on a public interest
basis.

(i) Can
Superbar assert Standing on the basis of Exceptional Prejudice?

[
33
]   Although other relief was requested, this case was treated both by
the Queen’s Bench and by this Court as an application for a declaration that s.
54(1)(b) offended
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
. But Superbar’s stance, and the
evidence led, indicate that Superbar seeks to strike down s. 54(1)(b) not on
the basis that it offends freedom of expression generally, but on the basis
that the dancers’ freedom of expression was curtailed by the regulation.
Superbar asserts it has standing because it could lose its licence to sell
alcoholic beverages under an unconstitutional law, but in light of the
evidentiary base it can only argue that the regulation is unconstitutional
because it offends the dancers’ freedom of expression.  It cannot seek standing
on the footing that any regulation prohibiting striptease offends the guarantee
of freedom of expression as a matter of course because no evidence was led to
support this proposition.  On the same basis, Superbar cannot say its own
freedom of expression was infringed.

[
34
]   Superbar is not “exceptionally prejudiced” by s. 54(1)(b)’s
prohibition against striptease performances in licensed premises. No one is
able to sell beverage alcohol in Saskatchewan unless they are licensed to do
so.  Section 135 of the
Act
provides:

135.     No person shall purchase beverage
alcohol from a person not authorized to sell beverage alcohol pursuant to this
Act or the regulations.

And no one who
sells beverage alcohol can offer striptease performances. Like everyone else in
Saskatchewan Superbar can offer striptease performances to the public but as a
holder of a liquor license, it just cannot offer liquor
and
strip tease
performances.  But no one else can either.  Contravention of this law means its
permit may be suspended and if Superbar persists, the Authority may move to
cancel its licence.  But is this any different from Mr. Smith who wanted to buy
liquor and could not?  Or Mr. Finlay who argued that his income security was
affected?  It is surely no different from the retailers in
Hy and Zel.’s

who were already facing criminal charges.

[
35
]   The majority and the minority in
Hy and Zel.’s
were in
agreement that the appellants were “directly affected” by the legislation under
attack.  Their businesses were regulated by the legislation under attack and
they and others had been charged under it in other proceedings and, presumably,
they and others faced future prosecutions. The minority said this constituted
“exceptional prejudice”, but the majority said it did not.

[
36
]   Superbar is part of a regulated system, but so were Big M Drug Mart
and Hy and Zel.’s.  Their status as part of a regulated system did not accord
them standing as of right.  Being part of a regulated system does not give one
automatic access to the courts to declare the system unconstitutional.
Entrance to the mercantile world in to-day’s society usually guarantees
regulation, but does not guarantee entitlement to strike down the system as
unconstitutional.  Something more is required.

[
37
]   Superbar’s real argument as a private interest litigant is that it
suffers a penalty because a third party’s rights are infringed by an
unconstitutional law, which raises for consideration whether Superbar is
entitled to standing in the same way Big M Drug Mart was granted standing. (See

R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto

(1977),
1997 CanLII 16226 (ON CA)
,
116 C.C.C. (3d) 1 (Ont.
C.A.)
at 52)
.

(ii) Can
Superbar assert Standing
on the basis of
Big M Drug Mart
?

[
38
]   Unlike Big M Drug Mart, Superbar was not charged with an offence
and nor could it be.
Section 142
of
The Alcohol and Gaming Regulation Act
,
which makes it possible for a person to be charged, on summary conviction, does
not apply to s. 54(1) of
The Alcohol Control Regulations
.  Section 54 of
the
Regulations
provides in its entirety:

54(1) It is a term and condition of every permit that
no permittee shall permit or allow in the permitted premises:

(a) any nude activity or entertainment; or

(b) any activity or entertainment that consists of a
striptease performance or wet clothing contest.

(2) Section 142 of the Act does not apply to any permittee
who contravenes subsection (1).

[
39
]   Presumably, s. 54(2) was passed pursuant to the power contained in
s. 179(b)(xxi.8) of the
Act,
which reads:

179 For the purposes of carrying out the provisions of
this Act according to their intent

(b) the Lieutenant Governor in Council may make
regulations

(xxi.8) exempting any person or category of persons
from this Act or any other provisions of this Act.

Since no party
asked the Court to consider the vires of any part of the regulations, we must
take it that Superbar was prohibited as a term of its permit from offering
striptease performances, but could not be charged with a summary conviction
offence if it did so.  Failure to comply with regulation  54(1)(b) could result
only in a suspension or a cancellation of its permit.  Subsection 18(6) of the
Act

provides the Liquor and Gaming Licensing Commission’s authority in this regard:

18(6) At a hearing conducted pursuant to this section,
the commission may suspend or cancel a license, permit or certificate of
registration where the commission is satisfied that:

(a) the licensee, permittee or registrant has violated
this Act, the regulations, any terms and conditions to which the licence,
permit or certificate of registration where the commission is satisfied that:

(a) the licensee, permittee or registrant has violated
this Act, the regulations, any terms and conditions to which the license,
permit or certificate of registration is subject or an order of the authority
or the commission; or

(b) it is not in the public interest that the licence,
permit or certificate of registration remain outstanding.

Thus the issue
becomes whether the threat of permit suspension or cancellation can be equated
with the possibility of being charged with a summary conviction offence so as
to extend the
Big M Drug Mart
doctrine.

[
40
]   The Supreme Court of Canada was given an opportunity to extend
Big
M Drug Mart
in
Hy and Zel.’s
and did not do so.  The retailers in
that case had an even closer claim to the status afforded Big M Drug Mart
because they had been charged, but chose to raise their constitutional question
by way of application.  If the retailers in
Hy and Zel.’s
could not come
within
Big M Drug Mart,
Superbar cannot do so either.

[
41
]   This interpretation accords with that taken by
the Ontario Court of
Appeal in
R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto
.  At their trial for
breach of trust, the Church of Scientology and an individual accused, who was a
non-citizen, challenged the constitutional validity of the jury selection
scheme in the
Juries Act
, R.S.O.  1990, c. J.3.  Under s. 2(b) of that
Act
,
only Canadian citizens are eligible for jury duty.  The accused argued that the
exclusion of non-citizens violated
ss. 7
,
11(d)
,(f) and
15
of the
Charter
.
The Court held that the doctrine
in
Big M Drug Mart

does not give the
accused the right to assert the personal rights of other actors in the
proceedings, except where the possible infringement of those rights affects the
accuseds’ rights (see p. 53).  To affect the accuseds’ rights, the Court said
they would have to demonstrate that the manner in which the jury panel was
selected infringed their rights as accused under s. 11(d) and (f) of the
Charter

which the Court concluded they were unable to do.  In reviewing the decisions
on this point from the Supreme Court of Canada Rosenberg J.A. said the common
thread is that because of their status as accused,  persons have been granted
standing to challenge the provisions under which they were charged, provided
the rights of some potential accused would be infringed (see p. 53).  Since no
one could be charged with an offence under the
Juries Act
, standing was
refused to challenge its validity.

[
42
]   Similarly, as I have demonstrated in this appeal, no one, including
the dancers, could be charged with an offence under the regulation in this
case.  Therefore, Superbar is not entitled to standing
on the basis of
Big M
Drug Mart
.

(iii) Is
Superbar entitled to Standing in the Public Interest?

[
43
]   Nor can Superbar succeed in asserting standing on a public interest
basis.  Cory J., speaking for a unanimous court
in
Canadian Council of
Churches
, wrote (at p. 253):

It has been seen that when public interest standing is
sought, consideration must be given to three aspects.  First, is there a
serious issue raised as to the invalidity of legislation in question?  Second,
has it been established that the plaintiff is directly affected by the
legislation or if not does the plaintiff have a genuine interest in its
validity?  Third, is there another reasonable and effective way to bring the
issue before the court?

(Major J. provided
a similar summary of the law in
Hy and Zel’s
at p. 690.)

[
44
]   Applying these criteria to the case at bar, there is no doubt that
a serious question as to the validity of s. 54(1)(b) has been raised. Superbar,
as a person regulated by the liquor licensing system in this province and
facing a suspension of its licence, is directly affected but its constitutional
rights are not.  We can, however, assume Superbar is directly affected, because
putting Superbar’s case at its highest still leaves the question of whether
there is another reasonable and effective way to bring this matter before the
Court.

[
45
]   To decide whether there is another reasonable and effective way to
challenge an unconstitutional law, it is appropriate to consider the nature of
the right said to be infringed.  The right said to be infringed is  “freedom of
expression” guaranteed by
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.
Clause 2(b)
provides:

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and
expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication.

[
46
]   Chief Justice Dickson summarized the values inherent in protecting
freedom of expression
in
Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec
.  He stated them to
be:  first, seeking and attaining truth; second, the fostering of participation
in social and political decision making; and third, individual self-fulfilment
(see: p. 976).  He defined expression in this way:

“Expression” has both a content and a form, and the
two can be inextricably connected.  Activity is expressive if it attempts to
convey meaning.  That meaning is its content.[at p. 968]

...Indeed, if the activity conveys or attempts to
convey a meaning, it has expressive content and
prima facie
falls within
the scope of the guarantee.  Of course, while most human activity combines
expressive and physical elements, some human activity is purely physical and
does not convey or attempt to convey meaning. [at p. 969]

But if a court
finds the activity to be expression, the court must still consider whether
the
effect
of the government’s action was to restrict expression or to attack
harmful physical consequences.  Dickson C.J. placed the burden squarely on the
complainant to demonstrate not only the meaning conveyed by the impugned
activity, but how it relates to the values protected by free expression:

To make this claim [that the effect of the
government’s action was to restrict expression] the plaintiff must at least
identify the meaning being conveyed and how it relates to the pursuit of truth,
participation in the community, or individual self-fulfilment and human
flourishing. [at p. 979]

In the case at bar
none of the dancers, even those employed by Superbar, testified.  And just as
in
Hy and Zel’s,
the evidence demonstrates that the dancers would be a
reasonable alternative means to test the validity of the regulation.  In this
case the Men of Extreme were not from Saskatchewan, but that would not prevent
them or those dancers resident in Saskatchewan from bringing an application.
Before a court grants public interest standing to one tavern owner on the basis
that there is no other reasonable and effective means of challenging the
regulation, the court must have evidence that the dancers will not or cannot
pursue the remedy on their own, and in light of
Irwin Toy
, their
evidence or the evidence of some surrogate who can testify as to meaning and
effect will be required.  In the result, Superbar is not entitled to public
interest standing.

[
47
]
Hy and Zel’s
has been criticized.  (See Peter Bowal &
Mark Cranwell in “Case Comment:
Persona Non Grata:
The Supreme Court of
Canada Further Constrains Public Interest Standing”, Alberta Law Review Vol.
XXXIII, No 1, 1994, p. 192 and June Ross, “Further Restrictions on access to
Charter

Review: A Comment on
Hy and Zel’s Inc. v. Ontario” (A.G.)
5
Constitutional Forum, Fall, 1994, p. 22). But as Cory J. demonstrated
in
Canadian
Council of Churches
(at pp. 242 to 248) Canada has the most liberal
standing rules of any of the democratic countries canvassed.  The difficulty is
developing a consistent, acceptable rationale for the grant or refusal of
standing that is in the public interest.

[
48
]   The traditional rationale for a law of standing which restricts
access to the Courts appears to have fallen by the wayside.  For example, no
one seriously contends that only the Attorney General should be able to question
the validity of legislation.  Similarly, in the absence of a “busybody”, the
floodgates argument is seen as an imperfect justification to withhold standing
in most cases in light of the costs and aggravation of litigation (
see
Canadian
Council of Churches
).

[
49
]   The modern rationale for granting or withholding standing relates
more to ensuring that an unconstitutional law will be challenged and to a
court’s responsibility to select the appropriate case to effect a challenge.
(See:  W.A. Bogart, “Standing and the
Charter
: Rights and Identity,” in Sharpe
(ed.),
Charter Litigation
(1987), at 1; Thomas Cromwell, “From Trilogy
to Quartet:
Minister of Finance of Canada v. Finlay
” (1987), 7 Windsor Y.B.
Access Justice 103.; and W.A. Bogart, Understanding Standing, Chapter IV:

Minister of Finance of Canada v. Finlay
” (1988), 10 Supreme Court L. Rev. 377.)

[
50
]   Indeed, our enhanced power under the
Charter
to find
legislation unconstitutional demands that we act in any appropriate case which
is plead before us, but we also must be sure we have the right case.  The
criteria developed by the Supreme Court in the cases which I have cited assist
the courts in finding the right case.  When a court is asked to exercise its
power to strike down legislation which is ultra vires the power of the
government---particularly where there is no settled legal or public
opinion---it must be satisfied that the applicant is someone who can properly
put the case which must be made.

[
51
]   If a court does not have the right litigant, the principles of
stare decisis and res judicata may result in error.  In the case at bar, we
might have concluded based on an incomplete evidentiary base that the dancers’
performance is not protectable “expression” within the meaning of s. 2(b) as
interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada.  This would not have advanced the
Charter
.
Such a conclusion may also have forestalled this Court, as a matter of binding
precedent, from deciding in a future case with better evidence that strip tease
performances constitute expression worth saving under the
Charter
.
Similarly, in the right case, if this were found to be expression, appropriate
s. 1 evidence may have an effect on the overall determination of whether the
regulation could be saved.

[
52
]   It is useful to consider Cory J.’s words, speaking for a unanimous
Court
in
Canadian Council of Churches
(at p. 252):

The whole purpose of granting status is to
prevent the immunization of legislation or public acts from any challenge.  The
granting of public interest standing is not required when, on a balance of
probabilities, it can be shown that the measure will be subject to attack by a
private litigant.  The principles for granting public standing set forth by
this Court need not and should not be expanded.  The decision whether to grant
status is a discretionary one with all that that designation implies.  Thus
undeserving applications may be refused.  Nonetheless, when exercising the
discretion the applicable principles should be interpreted in a liberal and
generous manner.

[
53
]   There is a natural inclination to grant standing to a litigant to have
a perplexing question resolved and to avoid the delays attendant upon waiting
for the “right” case.  But in reviewing the Supreme Court cases, where standing
has been granted, as the analysis of Rosenberg J.A. demonstrates
in
Church
of Scientology
,
(at p. 53) there is either a larger issue at stake or the
right of the third party is really, on fuller analysis, the right of the person
before the Court.  And where it is refused, the Court was seeking a different
litigant who would be better able to present the case required to be made.

[
54
]   A court must be careful when it withholds public interest standing
and be scrupulous as to its reasons for doing so.  Thomas A. Cromwell makes the
point in  “From Trilogy to Quartet:
Minister of Finance of Canada v. Finlay
”
(1987), 7
Windsor Yearbook of Access to Justice
103 at 114: “..a broad
discretion with regard to standing gives the courts a device either to avoid
matters which they wish to avoid or to reach questions they are anxious to
decide.”  But it is a discretion hedged about with many guiding principles
including a broad base of Supreme Court decisions.  Like cases will attract the
same treatment.  Superbar is more like Big M Drug Mart and Hy and Zel’s than
Messrs. Thorson, McNeil and Borowski who appeared to be acting in the public
interest with no more interest in the outcome than any other citizen.

[
55
]   Even in the process which brought Superbar to this Court, Superbar
did not act like a public interest litigant.  Its initial legal position was
not that this law infringed freedom of expression, but that its employees and
the Men of Extreme were not engaged in a striptease performance.  Then, before
us it would not agree to admit the s. 1 evidence which the Supreme Court of
Canada said in
R. v. Oakes

[1987] 1 S.C.R. 103
we must have to assess
properly a law said to be unconstitutional.  Superbar’s goal is a personal one
linked more to profit than genuine public interest.  It truly has a private
interest in this outcome.

[
56
]   This result does not affect
Re Elizabeth Fry Society of
Saskatchewan Inc. v. Saskatchewan (Legal Aid Commission)
(1989),
1988 CanLII 5217 (SK CA)
,
56 D.L.R.
(4th) 95 (Sask. C.A.)
.  In that case, it is clear that Elizabeth Fry had a
genuine interest in the outcome according to the Rules of Court.  It may be
taken there was evidence showing that the individual legal aid recipients who
may or may not have been able to pay the required contribution did not constitute
a reasonable and effective alternative to challenge the law.

[
57
]   I should also add that this result targets Superbar’s attempt to
have s. 54(1)(b) declared unconstitutional.  It does not affect any right
Superbar may have had to apply to quash the decision of the tribunal on other
grounds.

[
58
]   I have considered whether the standard of appellate review requires
me to accept the decision of the Queen’s Bench on standing.  The learned chambers
judge did not deal with the issue of standing in his reasons.  If it was argued
before him, I must conclude he decided that Superbar had standing as of right

in the
Smith
sense or under
Big M Drug Mart
or that he exercised
his discretion to grant public interest standing.  Given my interpretation of
the Supreme Court’s decisions, to have granted standing as of right would have
represented an error of law and therefore a decision under those bases would be
reviewable by this Court.

[
59
]   To review the discretionary ruling with respect to public interest
standing, I must be satisfied that the chambers judge erred in principle.  To
have granted public interest standing, the chambers judge would have had to
have found there were no other reasonable and effective way to challenge this
regulation.  Given my analysis, it is my view that there is another reasonable
and effective way which would permit the Court, given the nature of the right
said to have been infringed, to assess properly the challenged regulation.  If
it was not argued in the Queen’s Bench, the question of standing was argued
fully before us.

Effect of the
Lack of Evidence

[
60
]   Even if Superbar were to be granted standing, there is an
alternative basis on which this appeal must be allowed.

[
61
]   I have indicated above the need for a person asserting that some
activity is expression under the
Charter

to prove both the content and
the form.  As Chief Justice Dickson said
in
Irwin Toy Ltd.
(at p. 968),
an activity is expressive if it attempts to convey meaning and that meaning is
its content.

[
62
]   If someone’s freedom of expression has been infringed, it is not
that of Superbar, but that of the dancers. But there is no testimony from the
dancers.  How does a court determine the meaning which the dancers intended to
convey in the absence of their evidence or any evidence directed to the issue
of meaning?  This is especially important when one notes that exotic dancing is
not prohibited in Saskatchewan; it is only prohibited in licensed venues which
serve beverage alcohol.  Given the limits of this prohibition, i.e., a licensee
cannot serve alcohol with exotic dancing, it would be extremely pertinent to
know----as counsel for the Attorney General said---how the absence of alcohol
affects the freedom of expression of exotic dancers.  In the absence of this
evidence, it is not possible to determine whether the exotic dancing fell
within
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

[
63
]   Then, if it were to be found that the dancing falls within s. 2(b),

Irwin Toy
demonstrates the need to have the evidence of the dancers to
identify how the meaning being conveyed relates to the pursuit of truth,
participation in the community, or individual self-fulfilment, before a court
can conclude that freedom of expression has been curtailed.

[
64
]   This makes
Rio Hotel Ltd. v. New Brunswick (Liquor Licensing
Bd.)

1987 CanLII 72 (SCC)
,
[1987] 2 S.C.R. 59
applicable to the case at bar.  In
Rio
the
Supreme Court confirmed New Brunswick’s legislative competence to regulate nude
entertainment in taverns. Dickson C.J., writing for the majority of the Court,
wrote (at pp. 65 & 66):

...that the provincial legislation which authorizes
the impugned licence condition is intra vires the Legislature of New
Brunswick.  The legislation is, as I have stated, prima facie related to
property and civil rights within the Province and to matters of a purely local
nature.  The Legislature seeks only to regulate the forms of entertainment that
may be used as marketing tools by the owners of licensed premises to boost
sales of alcohol.  Although there is some overlap between the license condition
precluding nude entertainment and various provisions of the
Code
, there
is no direct conflict.  It is perfectly possible to comply with both the
provincial and the federal legislation.  Moreover, the sanction for breach of
the provincially-imposed licence conditions is suspension or cancellation of
the liquor licence.  No penal consequences ensue for the nude entertainer or
for the holder of the licence.  Under the relevant
Code
provisions, the
primary object is obviously to punish entertainers and proprietors who breach
the prohibitions on public nudity.  I cannot say that the federal
characteristics on this subject matter are palpably more important than the
provincial characteristics.  The provincial regulatory scheme relating to the sale
of the liquor, in the Province can, without difficulty, operate concurrently
with the
federal
Criminal Code
provisions.

Although the
majority and the minority (Estey and Lamer JJ.) arrived at this conclusion by
different means, all were agreed the case was not an appropriate one to
consider whether the regulation in question violated
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.
Estey J. wrote (at p. 83):

The record before the courts on this issue is woefully
inadequate and cannot serve as a base upon which to build an argument that this
law violates the above provision of the
Charter
.
The nature of the
conduct, said to amount to nude dancing, is not revealed in the record.  There
is no description of any such conduct, the extent of the alleged nudity, the
nature of the “expression” in question, or anything else of a factual nature
germane to this issue.  (
R.. v. Verrette,
1978 CanLII 208 (SCC)
,
[1978] 2 S.C.R. 838
).

The majority
agreed (see p.66).

[
65
]
Then in
Danson
v. Ontario (Attorney General)

1990 CanLII 93 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R. 1086
, the Supreme Court
considered whether an application for a declaration that certain rules of court
were unconstitutional could be considered if no facts were alleged by the
applicant in support of the relief claimed.  Sopinka J. for the Court said (at
p. 1093) “..the failure of a diffuse challenge could prejudice subsequent
challenges to the impugned rules by parties with specific and factually
established complaints.”  He concluded (at p. 1101):

The present case is, for these purposes, indistinguishable
from
MacKay,
and I would respectfully adopt and apply Cory J.’s comments
to these circumstances.  The appellant here seeks to attack the impugned rules
on the basis of their alleged effects upon the legal profession in Ontario.  It
would be, in my view, difficult if not impossible for a motions judge to assess
the merits of the appellant’s application under Rule 14.05(3)(h) without
evidence of these effects, by way of adjudicative facts (i.e., actual instances
of the use or threatened use of the impugned rule) and legislative facts (i.e.,
the purpose, history and perceptions among the profession of the impugned
rules).

Thus the Court
reaffirmed its position
articulated in
MacKay v. Manitoba
,
1989 CanLII 26 (SCC)
,
[1989] 2
S.C.R. 357
that any
Charter
challenge based upon allegations of the
unconstitutional effects of impugned legislation must be accompanied by
evidence.

[
66
]   When the learned chambers judge in the case at bar considered this
point, he distinguished
Rio
.  He said (at p. 180):

[47] In the matter before me, the record reveals the
nature, description and the extent of the alleged nudity as well as the nature
of the “expression” in question.  Thus, there is a base upon which argument may
be made whether the impugned section violates
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

But as in
Rio

there is nothing in the evidence summarized in Appendix “A” which speaks to the
meaning to be attributed to the expression or to the effect of the regulation
in the terms discussed in
Irwin Toy
.

[
67
]   There is no evidence directed to the message the dancers or any
other stripper real or hypothetical may have been trying to convey or how their
activity relates to the pursuit of truth, participation in the community, or
individual self-fulfilment and human flourishing.  All the evidence is directed
to the conduct of specific dancers.  This is understandable because when this
evidence was led it was not directed to the issue before the Court; rather it
was directed to whether the activity was in fact a striptease performance.

[
68
]   Without the dancers’ evidence or any other evidence addressed to
the point, we are forced to consider in the abstract---to speculate---what the
content or the message of a striptease performance might be.

[
69
]   We might be able to determine meaning by consulting texts and
dictionaries, but counsel did not direct us to any such material.  Moreover, it
seems somewhat inconsistent for the Court to be able to consult external
sources not cited to it to determine the meaning and the effects of the
prohibition against strip tease performances when Superbar’s counsel did not
want the Court to consider the evidence provided by counsel for the Attorney
General which was intended to determine the purpose and worth of the
regulation.

[
70
]   There is another danger in considering strip tease performance in
the abstract.  We have no evidence of what constitutes the “normal” strip tease
performance in taverns.  Does it take different forms? Is it usually men or is
it usually women who act as strippers?  Are there differences between the two
types of performances?  Assuming a different performance, is the audience
affected differently?  If we consider the abstract performance in the absence
of even this type of evidence, we will strike down s. 54(1)(b) for all purposes
when there may be some forms of such performance less expressive and more
egregious than others.

[
71
]   Saskatchewan has a long history of controlling the sale and
consumption of alcoholic beverages. Given the way this case evolved without the
testimony of the dancers or any evidence relating to strip tease performance
and in the absence of s. 1 evidence demonstrating the appropriateness of this
regulation, this is not the case where the Court should play a role in changing
such laws.

[
72
]   For the foregoing reasons, I would allow the appeal with costs to
the Commission and the Crown, if asked for.

[
78
]   The central question on this appeal is whether a provincial
government regulation banning "entertainment containing a strip tease
performance" in nightclubs permitted to sell alcohol is invalid as being
inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution of Canada guaranteeing
freedom of expression.

1.
The Facts

[
79
]   The case arose out of an order made by the Alcohol and Gaming
Licensing Commission, a branch of the Saskatchewan Liquor and Gaming
Authority.  The Commission ordered the suspension of a permit issued by the
Authority to the owner of "The Great Canadian Superbar," a Saskatoon
restaurant, lounge, and night-club. The permit allowed the owner to sell and
serve beverage alcohol on the premises. The Commission made the order following
a performance in the nightclub by a Toronto dance troupe, a four man group of
professional body builders known as "The Men of Extreme."

[
80
]   The performance took place during a "Special Edition Ladies
Night," restricted to women.  Typically, each of the men appeared on stage
in full costume--dressed as a Russian Cossack, for example, or as James
Bond--and danced to selected music for about 20 minutes. While doing so, each
removed his clothing down to his "briefs" or "shorts," but
not beyond. Some of the women then stuffed money into the waistbands of the
men's briefs. The performers were described by a senior liquor inspector,
present to monitor the activity, as "very good athletes" whose
dancing was not uncommon, except for the removal of their clothing.

[
81
]   In preparation for this event, which formed part of a "Grand
Opening" promotion following a change of ownership, the manager of the
night-club advised the troupe they were to keep their groin areas and buttocks
covered and to refrain from lewd behaviour. Indeed the manager had the group
sign a written undertaking to this effect.  He knew the Liquor and Gaming
Authority had been keeping an eye on the night-club's entertainment and would
have a representative present. In fact, the Authority had received a complaint
from a competitor and had a senior inspector meet with the manager in advance
of the event for the purpose of discussing this and past performances of male
dancers on "ladies nights."

[
82
]   The nature of the past performances is unclear, except in general,
for the evidence before the Commission in this respect was contradictory and
the Commission made few findings of fact. But the earlier performances also
featured male dancers who removed their clothing--Chippendale attire for the
most part--down to articles covering their groin areas. No nudity, nor anything
else of note, occurred during any of the performances.

[
83
]   The Commission suspended the permit pursuant to section 18(6)(a) of

The Alcohol and Gaming Regulation Act
, S.S., c. A-18.01. This section
empowers the Commission to take action of this nature if satisfied a permit
holder "has violated the Act, the regulations, any terms or conditions to
which the...permit...is subject, or an order of the authority or the
commission."

[
84
]   Both the
Act
and
The Alcohol Control Regulations, 1994

ban certain activity in establishments permitted to sell beverages containing
alcohol.

Section 131(1) of
the
Act
does so in these terms:

131(1) No permittee shall permit or allow any
entertainment, game, sports, or other activity on any premises with respect to
which a permit has been issued that:

(a) is unlawful;

(b) may be detrimental to the orderly operation of the
premises;

(c) has been prohibited by the municipality in which
the premises are located;

(d) is prescribed in the regulations.

Section 54(1) of
the
Regulations
is more explicit:

54(1) It is a term and condition of every permit that
no permittee shall permit or allow in the permitted premises:

(a) any nude activity or entertainment; or

(b) any activity or entertainment that contains a
strip tease performance or wet clothing contest.

[
85
]   A violation of any of these provisions constitutes a potentially
serious matter, empowering the Commission, acting under section 18(6) of the
Act,

to suspend or cancel the violator's permit.  A violation of any of them
also constitutes a summary conviction offence, according to section 142 of the
Act,

empowering the Provincial Court to fine or imprison the offender.

[
86
]   Satisfied the owner of the night-club had violated that part of
section 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations
which prohibits "entertainment
that contains a strip tease performance," the Commission suspended the
owner's beverage alcohol permit for two successive weekends.

[
87
]   At that, the owner applied to the Court of Queen's Bench for
judicial review, requesting an order from the Court quashing the suspension on
one ground or another, including the ground the regulation underpinning the
suspension was unconstitutional.

2.
The
Application to the Court of Queen's Bench

(1)
The Nature of the Application

[
88
]   So far as the application rested on constitutional grounds, it
sought to have the suspension quashed on the basis the regulation upon which
the Commission had relied in suspending the owner's liquor permit--subsection
54(1)(b) of the
Regulations
--was invalid under
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
:

52(1) The Constitution of Canada is the supreme law of
Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution is to the extent of the inconsistency of no force or effect.

[
89
]   The regulation was alleged to be inconsistent with two provisions
of the Constitution: First, with
section 91(27)
of the
Constitution Act,
1867
,
which confers upon Parliament exclusive legislative authority over
the criminal law; and, second, with section 2(b) of the
Charter

of
Rights and Freedoms,
which protects freedom of expression in these terms:

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and
expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication
.

[
90
]   In the light of these provisions of the Constitution, the
regulation was said to be inconsistent therewith for one or the other of the
following reasons:

First, because it concerned public nudity and
indecency, matters of "criminal law" that are not only assigned to
the exclusive           legislative authority of Parliament under
section
91(27)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

but are already covered by the
Criminal
Code

in
section 174
.

Second, because it limited freedom of expression, as
protected by
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

[
91
]   In either event, it was said that the regulation was invalid having
regard for
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982

and that in
consequence the Commission did not have the power to make the order it did.

[
92
]   It might be noted that the application sought to have the order of
the Commission quashed on the basis the regulation was invalid in its entirety,
even though the order was founded not upon the whole but only upon a portion of
the impugned regulation.  The order was founded upon that portion of subsection
54(1)(b) of the
Regulations
which prohibits "entertainment that
contains a strip tease performance."  The Commission did not act upon
those parts banning "any activity" of this nature or "any
activity or entertainment that contains...a wet clothing contest."
Accordingly, those parts were irrelevant and the application was overdrawn to the
extent it suggested that they, too, were inconsistent with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter

and of no force or effect under
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
.

[
93
]   It might also be noted that, since the Commission had not acted

Regulations,
banning "any nude
activity or entertainment," the application did not touch this part of the
subsection.

[
94

issue and fell to be treated as being fully effective. It was only the
constitutional validity of that portion of subsection 54(1)(b) banning
"entertainment that contains a striptease performance" that was at
issue. And so the application raised a much narrower case than was generally

[
95
]   Notice of the application was served upon the Attorney General, as
required by subsection 8(2) of
The Constitutional Questions Act
, S.S.
C-29. This is required for the dual purpose of enabling the Attorney General to

attack upon the constitutional validity of section 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations

and informed of the grounds for the attack.

[
96
]   The Attorney General chose not to appear, however, leaving the
defence of the regulation to the Commission.  In the main, the Commission
defended the constitutional validity of the regulation on two grounds:

First, that its enactment fell within the powers
conferred upon the Province by
sections 92(13)
and
(16)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
(to legislate in relation to "property and civil
rights" and to "matters of purely local concern") and did not
conflict with the
Criminal Code
.

Second, that it did not amount to a limit upon the

section 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

(2)
The Order of the Court of Queen's Bench

[
97
]   The application came before Mr. Justice Hrabinsky. It was
accompanied by extensive briefs, or written arguments, exchanged by counsel in
advance of the hearing in compliance with a court order to that effect. The
order appears to have been made to the ends of ensuring a clear identification

As might be expected, the briefs dealt at some length with each of the two

[
98
]   In delivering his judgment, Mr. Justice Hrabinsky expressly
addressed each of these limbs, turning first to the attack based upon
section
91(27)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.

[
99
]   Having regard for the decision of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Rio
Hotel Ltd
. v.
New Brunswick (Liquor Licensing Bd.)
,
1987 CanLII 72 (SCC)
,
[1987]  2 S.C.R.
59
, he agreed with the Commission that the regulation was not unconstitutional

the Province by
sections 92(13)
and
(16)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

and
was not incompatible with the
Criminal Code
. (In
Rio Hotel
, the
Supreme Court held that a provincial law prohibiting "nude

division of powers under
sections 91
and
92
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.

Charter

[
100
] Mr. Justice Hrabinsky then turned to the second limb of the attack

section 2(b)
of
the
Charter
. Having regard for the decision of
the Supreme Court of
Canada in
Irwin Toy Ltd
. v.
Quebec
,
1989 CanLII 87 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 927
, he
identified two issues: Whether the activity of the dancers constituted

Regulations
was to
limit expression.

[
101
] As for the first, he took the view, based on the decision in

Toy
, that physical activity, if it conveys or attempts to convey meaning,

section.  Being of that view, and satisfied the performances in question

s. 2(b)
of the
Charter

[
102
] With that, he turned to the purpose and effect of section 54(1)(b) of
the
Regulations
with a view to determining if it limited the freedom of
such expression. Having regard, once again, for the decision in
Irwin Toy,

took up this issue on the premise that if a law be aimed at controlling an

in
R.
v.
Ludacka

(1996),
1996 CanLII 401 (ON CA)
,
105 C.C.C. (3d) 565 (Ont. C.A.)
, where female entertainers in a bar

Alcohol Control Regulations, 1994

consequences of this human activity, no matter what meaning is being conveyed,

effect of the impugned section is to restrict the content of expression, or to

s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

Having made these
findings, he wrapped up his consideration of these matters, saying:

It has not been shown that s. 154(1)(b) of the
Regulations can be demonstrably justified under
s. 1
of the
Charter
. I
find that s. 54 (1)(b) of
The Alcohol and Control Regulations, 1994

contravenes
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and
is therefore void and of no force or effect.

(1)
Standing

[
107
] To the extent the first ground of appeal suggests the owner's
standing to claim that the impugned regulation was unconstitutional, having

sections 2(b)
of the
Charter
and 52(1) of the
Constitution
Act 1982
