locus
standi,
was brought into question.  Nor do I believe Mr. Justice Hrabinsky
determined any such matter. And so I rather think this ground of appeal is
misconceived. In any event, however, I can see no tenable basis upon which this
Court could set aside the order of the Court of Queen's Bench on the ground the
owner lacked standing to claim that the impugned regulation was
unconstitutional having regard for section 2(b) of the
Charter

[
108
] The term
locus standi
, as it applies to legal proceedings, is
succinctly defined in
Black's Law Dictionary
(5th ed.) to mean:

A place of standing; standing in court. A right of
appearance in a court of justice...on a given question.

[
109
] Roughly speaking, this place of standing, enabling a person to appear
before and be heard by a court in relation to a given question, may be acquired
in one of two ways: As of right, in reliance upon one's own private interests
in the question ("private interest standing"); or with leave of the
court, in reliance largely upon the public's interest in the question
("public interest standing").  And standing may exist, or be granted,
in both civil and criminal proceedings, proceedings of one sort or another
involving claims of various kinds, including a claim that a law is
unconstitutional.

[
110
] Standing in relation to claims that a law is unconstitutional rests
upon a more extensive foundation of principle than usual, one that is more
liberal because of some of the ideas underlying this branch of the law. This is
explained with clarity by Professor Hogg in Chapter 56 of his text
Constitutional
Law of Canada
(Loose-leaf Edition). He notes at p. 56-3:

The question whether a person has 'standing' (or
locus
standi
) to bring legal proceedings is a question about whether the person
has a sufficient stake in the outcome to invoke the judicial process. The
question of standing focuses on the position of the party seeking to sue, not
on the issues that the lawsuit is intended to resolve.

He goes on to note
that standing in constitutional cases rests upon an idea unique to this
field--the idea of "constitutionalism (or rule of law), which dictates
that remedies ought to be available when governments fail to abide by the law
of the constitution":

This idea often suggests that a private litigant who,
for public rather than private interest reasons, wishes to raise a
constitutional question ought to be allowed to do so. This is probably the
reason for the remarkable relaxation in the Canadian law of public interest
standing....

Then, in turning
briefly to private interest standing, he adds:

Where a constitutional issue arises in the course of
ordinary civil or criminal litigation, a question of standing is rarely
controversial. The validity of a statute (or some other official instrument or
act) must be determined in order to resolve the issue between the parties. It
goes without saying that only the party who would be affected by the
application of the statute has any right to raise the issue of its
constitutionality. That person has standing to attack the validity of the
statute.

[
111
] Seen in this light, the issue in the Court of Queen's Bench, had the
matter been raised there, would have been whether the night-club owner was in a
position, either as of right or with leave of the Court, to appear and be heard
in respect of the second of the constitutional questions raised by the owner's
application for judicial review of the decision of the Commission, the second
question being this: Is the regulation upon which the Commission founded its
decision to suspend the owner's permit unconstitutional on the basis it is
inconsistent with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
and therefore of no force
or effect under
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
?

[
112
] This, in my judgment, is the basic nature of the matter under
consideration. And as such, I do not believe it was raised in the Court of
Queen's Bench. I say that for several reasons. To begin with, the record of the
proceedings in that Court suggests that standing in the sense of
locus
standi
was not brought into question. The written briefs exchanged in
advance of the hearing of the application neither identify this as an issue nor
address it. Nor do Mr. Justice Hrabinsky's rather lengthy reasons for judgment
make any mention of this. And the record contains no ruling or order made by
him in this connection. Indeed the order against which the appeal is taken
contains no disposition of any such issue.

[
113
] In the light of all this, coupled with the threshold nature of
locus
standi,
it appears this was not brought into question in the Court of
Queen's Bench but was raised for the first time on appeal. And absent any
ruling or order of the Court of Queen's Bench in this respect, it is difficult
to find the foundation for this ground of appeal.

[
114
] When asked about this, counsel for the Authority contended that the
matter had been brought into question in the Court of Queen's Bench, referring
us to a passage appearing in the Commission's written argument, or brief, filed
in advance of the hearing in compliance with the order of the Court to that
effect. With respect, I think this contention rests on a misunderstanding of
the basic nature of the matter. And I do not think the passage, when read in
context, supports counsel's contention.

[
115
] The Commission's brief, having canvassed the facts of the case and a
number of other legal issues, then addresses "The Attack on Regulation
54(b)," dealing in turn with the constitutional attack based first upon
the division of governmental powers and then upon the provisions of
section
2(b)
of the
Charter
. The portion of the brief dealing with section 2(b)
of the
Charter
opens with these statements:

The Applicants also attack this Regulation on the
basis it infringes upon their freedom of expression. We concede that this
Regulation must be tested against the
Canadian Charter
of Right and
Freedoms,
and must withstand the challenge. In other words, if the court
concludes that this is an improper restriction or prohibition on the freedom of
expression, that the Regulation must be struck down. It is our position,
however, that there is no infringement upon the freedom of expression.

[
116
] What follows is a request of the Court, in thus testing the
regulation, to bear in mind "a few particularly important facts,"
including the fact that the applicant is not a professional dancer; that it's
business is the operation of a licensed liquor outlet; and that the impugned
regulation does not prohibit the applicant's pursuit of its livelihood, but
only restricts its ability to market its business through entertainment or
activity of the nature of that prohibited by the regulation:

As a result, we respectfully submit that the
Applicants cannot argue that their freedom of expression has in any way been
denied. Rather the Applicants appear to be in the position where they claim the
right to vicariously argue an infringement of the freedom of expression on
behalf of the dance troupe that they contracted with. In such a situation, we
respectfully submit that the court should not entertain the argument based upon

section 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

This is the
passage relied upon by counsel in contending
locus standi
had been
brought into question. The passage is followed by extensive argument concerning
the construction and application of section 2(b). No where does the written
brief mention private or public interest standing, or analyse these matters, or
cite any authority concerning them.

[
117
] With respect, it seems to me this passage amounts to a summary point
of argument made in the context of the opening statements setting forth the
general position to be taken by the Commission on this branch of the case,
including its understanding of the fundamental basis of the claim being made by
the owner:
that the regulation infringed the owner's freedom of expression
.
The claim, which was not founded on
section 24(1)
of the
Charter
, was
actually broader than this, but the essence of the point being made by the
Commission seems to be that the court, in determining the claim, should
remember that it is the
owner's
freedom of expression, not that of
the
dancer's
, that is in issue and that in the circumstances the owner's
freedom of expression cannot be seen to have been infringed.

[
118
] Even if this is not quite the point of argument being made by the
Commission, still I do not think this passage can be see to have placed the
locus
standi
of the applicant into issue in relation to the question of whether
the regulation was inconsistent with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
and
therefore of no force or effect under section 52(1) of the
Constitution Act
.
Indeed, standing in relation to this question appears to have been conceded. It
is certainly difficult to make anything else out of the opening statement:
"We concede that this Regulation must be tested against the
Canadian
Charter of Right and Freedoms
, and must withstand the challenge."

[
119
] In the light of all of this it is not surprising to me that Mr.
Justice Hrabinsky did not address
locus standi
in his reasons for
judgment--with a view, of course, to determining whether the owner might appear
before him and be heard, either as of right or with leave, in connection with
the constitutional question founded upon
sections 2(b)
of the
Charter

and 52(1) of the
Constitution Act, 1982
.

[
120
] This is not as it should be and makes for difficulty. Indeed, appellate
courts rarely entertain grounds of appeal which bring into question matters of
this nature for the first time--matters which had they been raised earlier
might have altered the course of the proceedings by attracting the introduction
of other evidence, for example, or the addition of other parties.

[
121
] Moreover, appellate courts are given to reviewing decisions for
error, making it awkward for them to deal with matters of this kind when raised
for the first time on appeal. Involving as it does the exercise of
discretionary power vested in the Court of Queen's Bench to grant standing
where it does not exist as of right, this matter falls to be taken up on an
appellate standard reserved for reviewing the exercise of such powers. That
standard rests upon the two-fold premise that the operative discretion is
vested in the Court of Queen's Bench, not in the Court of Appeal, and that the
function of the Court of Appeal, at least at the outset, is one of review only,
review for error vitiating the exercise in the Court of Queen's Bench of that
discretion:
Sask. Power Corp.
v.
Doe
, [1986] 6 W.W.R. 634.

[
122
] And so I harbour grave doubts about taking up the first ground of
appeal. Indeed I am of the opinion it is misconceived and should not be
entertained. But even if it were otherwise, I might say I am not satisfied that
the owner lacked standing in relation to the question at issue, or could not
have been granted standing by Justice Hrabinsky in the exercise by him of his
discretionary power in this connection.

[
123
] Whether standing might appropriately have been accorded the
night-club owner in the Court of Queen's Bench, either as of right or grace,
has to do with whether the owner was in a position to invoke
section 2(b)
of
the
Charter

in support of its application,
having regard for the
nature of both the interests at stake and the proceedings in play.
And so
it is important to maintain a clear view of the whole of the context in which
section 2(b) of the
Charter
was invoked.

(a) the context in which section 2(b) was raised

[
124
] Generally speaking, the owner applied to the Court of Queen's Bench
claiming that the Commission had suspended its liquor permit; that the
Commission did not have the power to do so; and that the Court was empowered to
remedy the situation by setting aside the suspension. The application was
launched on these footings, including the immediate, concrete, personal
interest of the owner in the outcome of the proceedings, an interest founded at
bottom on the loss of its permit for a violation of subsection 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations
.

[
125
] The application was made on the authority of Rules 664 to 676 of
The
Queen's Bench Rules
governing proceedings for "Judicial Review."
Hence it was aimed at the Court's supervisory jurisdiction--its inherent
authority as a superior court to supervise the exercise of power by public
officials and tribunals. In effect the application requested the Court to
review the decision of the Commission by way of
certiorari
with an eye
to determining if, as claimed by the owner, the Commission had not been
effectively empowered to suspend the owner's liquor permit on the basis it did.
The application went on to request a remedy, in the event the Court concluded
that the Commission lacked such power, a discretionary remedy available on
judicial review by way of
certiorari
, namely an order of the Court
quashing the order of the Commission.

[
126
] It was within this external framework of general law, and with this
personal interest of the owner at stake, that the application raised the
several provisions of the Constitution of Canada in question, namely
section
52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, rendering laws inconsistent with
the Constitution of Canada invalid;
section 91(27)
of the
Constitution Act,
1867
, placing power over the criminal law in the hands of the federal
government and preventing encroachment by the provincial governments; and
section 2(b) of the
Charter of Rights and Freedoms,
placing freedom of
expression beyond the power of both levels of government and preventing
encroachment by either, subject only to
section 1
of the
Charter
.

[
127
] In the light of this, the application for judicial review rested upon
the internal premise the regulation empowering the Commission to make the order
it did was of no force or effect pursuant to
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
, because the regulation concerned subject matter that was placed
beyond the legislative and executive power of the Province by either
section 91

of the
Constitution Act, 1867
or
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

[
128
] It should be emphasized, perhaps, that this was an application for
judicial review of an administrative tribunal's decision adversely affecting
the economic interests of the applicant, not an action for a declaration based
upon a general interest in the validity of the impugned regulation. And the
application was not made pursuant to
section 24(1)
of the
Charter
, which
enables someone whose
section 2(b)
freedom of expression has been infringed or
denied to apply to the Court of Queen's Bench for an appropriate remedy. Indeed
the application did not invoke section 24(1).

[
129
] Rather, the application was made pursuant to the general law and
invoked
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
.
Unlike section
24(1), which operates in relation only to the
Charter
and its breach,

section 52(1)
operates in relation to the whole of the Constitution of Canada
and its contravention, including the
Constitution Act, 1867
and the
Charter
of Rights and Freedoms.
This not only empowers the courts, when properly
called upon to determine constitutional questions, to treat as invalid any law
that contravenes either of these constitutional provisions, but requires that
they do so:
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
[1985] 1 S.C.R. 295
.

[
130
] It was in this context, then, including the personal stake of the
owner in the outcome of the proceedings and the idea of "constitutionalism
(or rule of law)," that the application raised both
section 91(27)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
and
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
. And, of course, it is
this that underlies the question of whether, had the matter of private standing
been brought into question in the Court of Queen's Bench, Mr. Justice Hrabinsky
might properly have taken the owner to have had such standing.

(b)    Could the owner not have been held entitled

to private interest standing?

[
131
] To begin with, it might be noted that the owner was undoubtedly
entitled as a matter of private interest standing to challenge the validity of
the regulation on the basis it was inconsistent with
section 91(27)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
.
The courts have long operated on the non-controversial notion
that persons directly and adversely affected by government action based in a
law that might be constitutionally invalid, having regard for the division of
powers under the
Constitution Act, 1867,
are entitled to make such
claims and to call upon the courts to hear and determine them:
Labour
Relations Board for Sask
. v.
John East Iron Works Ltd
.
1948 CanLII 266 (UK JCPC)
,
[1949] AC
134
; [1948] 2 W.W.R. 1055, and
Central Canada Potash Co
. v.
Gov't of
Sask.

1978 CanLII 21 (SCC)
,
[1979] 1 S.C.R. 42
.

[
132
] The first of these cases arose, as did the case now before us, out of
an application for judicial review by way of
certiorari
of the decision
of an administrative tribunal empowered by provincial enactment to make orders
affecting the economic interests of persons engaged in a sphere of commercial
activity. The case involved a decision of the Saskatchewan Labour Relations
Board, a tribunal charged with overseeing this field of activity within the
Province. On a complaint by the United Steel Workers of America, the Board

found that
John East Iron Works Limited
of Saskatoon had committed an unfair
labour practice in dismissing several of its employees, contrary to
The
Trade Union Act
,
1944
, 2nd sess., ch. 69. In consequence, the Board
ordered the company to reinstate the employees and reimburse them for lost
wages.

[
133
] The company then applied for judicial review of the decision by way
of
certiorari
, asking that the orders of the Board be quashed on the
basis the provisions of the
Trade Union Act, 1944
empowering the Board
to make such orders were invalid because they were inconsistent with
section 96

of the
Constitution Act, 1867
(formerly the
British North America
Act, 1867).
The application was made to this Court, rather than the Court
of Queen's Bench, and the Court entertained it, never doubting the company's
standing, which is to say the company's right to appear and be heard in
relation to this constitutional question. Indeed the case eventually ended up
in the Privy Council on this basis.

[
134
] The case stands for the general proposition that a person whose
economic interests have been directly and adversely affected by the decision of
an administrative tribunal is entitled to apply to the courts for judicial
review, by way of
certiorari
, on the footing the decision rests upon an
unconstitutional enactment. This is not to say that a person in this position
is entitled to this remedy, for the remedy is discretionary, but it is to say
that such a person is entitled to be before the court and to be heard.

[
135
] Obviously, there appears to be little, if anything, to distinguish
the present case from the one before this Court in
John

East Iron
Works.
The owner's stake in the outcome of the proceedings, based on the
nature and extent of the interests underlying its claim, is essentially no
different. Nor is there any difference in the make-up of the proceedings or the
nature of the sought-after remedy. Indeed the only difference is that the
enactment at issue in
John East Iron Works
was said to be
unconstitutional because it was inconsistent with section 96 of what is now the

Constitution Act, 1867
, whereas in this case the enactment at issue was
alleged to have been inconsistent with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
. In
itself, however, this is inconsequential because
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
is equally applicable to legislative inconsistencies with the
provisions of the
Constitution Act, 1867
and the
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms.

[
136
]

On what basis, then, might the night-club owner be thought to
lack private interest standing in respect of the constitutional question
centred on
sections 2(b)
of the
Charter
and 52(1) of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
?  In other words, how could the owner be taken, at once, to have
been entitled to advance its claim that the regulation was unconstitutional as
being inconsistent with
section 91(27)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
,
and not to have been entitled to pursue its claim that the regulation was
unconstitutional as being inconsistent with section 2(b) of the
Charter
?

[
137
] The Authority and the Attorney General submitted, in effect, that the
owner was not entitled to do so for the reason, first, that the freedom of
expression of only the dancers, not that of the owner, could conceivably have
been affected by the regulation; and second, that the owner had not been
charged with an offence, a prerequisite to
locus standi
when only the
rights or freedoms of others are affected by an allegedly unconstitutional
enactment:
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart
. With respect, I do not agree
with either proposition.

[
138
] As for the first, I think the
owner's
freedom of expression,
not just that of the dancers, was potentially affected by the regulation. By
potentially affected I mean adversely affected should performances of the
nature banned by the regulation prove, as alleged, to fall within the scope of

section 2(b)
of the
Charter
. I think the owner's freedom of expression
was potentially affected, because the regulation prohibited the owner, as the
proprietor of the establishment and the holder of a permit, from allowing
striptease performances in its establishment. On the face of it, then, the
regulation prohibited the owner from doing what it did, namely allowing
performances such as that of the Men of Extreme, performances commissioned by
and performed on the premises of the owner in accordance with its directions.

[
139
] To suggest this did not engage the owner's freedom of expression, but
only that of the performers--assuming the performances fell within the scope of
section 2(b) of the
Charter
--is to suggest, for example, that a theatre
owner is not exercising its freedom of expression in sponsoring a performance
or presenting a film; that a gallery owner has no freedom of expression
interest of its own in displaying a sculptor's works; and that a newspaper is
not employing its freedom of speech in publishing a journalist's column. Is the
Saskatoon Star Phoenix reliant upon the author's freedom of speech in freely
publishing his or her writing without restraint by government regulation?  I do
not think so.

[
140
] But even if the night-club owner's freedom of expression was not
directly affected, as such, by the regulation, I do not
see
R.
v.
Big
M Drug Mart
as denying the owner private interest standing, in circumstances
such as these, to claim the impugned regulation was unconstitutional on the
combined basis of
sections 2(b)
of the
Charter
and 52(1) of the
Constitution
Act, 1982.

[
141
]

In
Big M Drug Mart
,
a Sunday shopping case, the Supreme
Court of Canada held that the company, having been charged with doing business
on that day contrary to the
Lord's Day Act
, was entitled to defend the
charge on the basis the
Act
was inconsistent with
section 2(a)
of the
Charter

and unconstitutional under
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
.

Section 2(a)
protects freedom of conscience and religion. Since only
individuals and not corporations are capable of possessing such freedom, it had
been argued that the company was in no position to claim that the
Act

was unconstitutional on this basis.

[
142
] Addressing the issues of standing to which this situation gave rise,
Chief Justice Dickson observed that:

Standing and jurisdiction to challenge the validity of
a law pursuant to which one is being prosecuted is the same regardless of
whether that challenge is with respect to
ss. 91
and
92
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
or with respect to the limits imposed on the legislatures by the
Constitution
Act, 1982
[including
section 2
of the
Charter
]. [p.313]

The Court rejected
the idea that the company, devoid of freedom of expression and unable to draw
upon any such interest of its own, did not have standing to defend the charge
on the footing the enactment was unconstitutional on the basis of
sections 2(a)

of the
Charter
and 52(1) of the
Constitution Act, 1982
. The Court
noted that the company had not invoked
section 24(1)
of the
Charter
, the
remedial provisions of which are only available to someone whose own rights or
freedoms have been infringed or denied, and that anyone charged with the
commission of a criminal offence, corporate or individual, is entitled to
defend the charge on the basis the law under which the charge is brought is
unconstitutional: "No one can be convicted of an offence under an
unconstitutional law," it was said (p.313).

[
143
] If anything, this decision took an expansive rather than a restricted
view of standing, allowing the company to invoke
sections 2(a)
of the
Charter

and 52(1) of the
Constitution Act, 1982
in defence of the charge even
though the company, in doing business on Sunday, could not possibly have been
engaged in the exercise of freedom of religion. To have done otherwise would
have been unthinkable, for otherwise someone could be convicted of violating
the provisions of an unconstitutional law. That is plain to see. Is it not
equally plain to see that no one should be deprived of a license or permit for
violating an unconstitutional law?

[
144
] This much is certain: had the night-club owner been charged under

section 142
of
The Alcohol and Gaming Regulation Act
with breaching
subsection 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations,
there could have been no
doubting the owner's standing as of right--its private interest standing--to
have raised the constitutional question it did and to have been heard in
respect of that question:
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart
. (See, also,
R.

v.
Westfair Foods Ltd
.,
1989 CanLII 5131 (SK CA)
,
65 D.L.R. (4th) 56 (Sask.C.A.)
, where the
company successfully invoked
section 2
(a) in defence of charge of contravening
a Saskatoon bylaw regulating Sunday shopping).

[
145
]
Section 142
of
The Alcohol and Gaming Regulation Act
provides
as follows:

142  A person who contravenes any provision of this
Act or the

regulations...is guilty of an offence and liable on
summary conviction

[to]:

(a) a fine of:

(i) not more than $10,000.00 for an
individual;

( ii) not more than $50,000.00 for a corporation;

(b) imprisonment for a term of not more
than six months;

(c) both the fine and imprisonment in
clauses (a) and (b).

[
146
] Rather than charge the owner under this section of the
Act,

charging it with the summary conviction offence of contravening subsection
54(1)(b) of the
Regulations,
the authorities laid a complaint against
the owner under section 18 of the
Act
, a complaint accusing the owner of
having violated subsection 54(1)(b).  Hence the owner was exposed not to a fine
but to the suspension or cancellation of its liquor permit. That being so,
according to the submissions of the Authority and the Attorney General, the
owner was in no position to claim that the regulation was inconsistent with

section 2(b)
of the
Charter

and unconstitutional under
section 52(1)
of
the
Constitution Act, 1982
. The owner could only have done so, in their
submission, had it been charged with the commission of an offence--with
violating section 142, in other words, for this is the only provision of the
statute creating such an offence.

[
147
] But the owner could not have been charged with an offence under
section 142 of the
Act
, not in the submission of the Authority and the
Attorney General, for subsection 54(2) of the
Regulations
foreclosed
that possibility. Subsection 54(2) of the
Regulations
, which appears
immediately after subsections 54(1)(a) and (b) prohibiting nudity, strip tease,
and wet clothing contests, reads thus:

54(2) Section 142 of the Act does not apply to any
permittee who contravenes subsection (1).

[
148
] This surely constitutes a rare, if not unique, exercise of the power
accorded by the Act to the Lieutenant Governor in Council to enact regulations
"for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this Act according to
their intent."  Whether or not the provision was intended to operate in a
manner suggested by the submissions of the Authority and the Attorney
General--to shield subsections 54(1)(a) and (b) of the
Regulations
from
constitutional attack--it is of questionable validity.

[
149
] But that is neither here nor there for the purpose at hand, because
in assessing
locus standi
in situations such as these there can be no
meaningful distinction between the position of a person faced, on the one hand,
with a summary conviction offence and an order to pay a fine for contravening
subsection 54(1)(b), and on the other, with a grave regulatory violation and an
order suspending or cancelling a permit for contravening the subsection. In my
opinion, the latter is the functional equivalent of the former, and it would
defeat the ends of justice to deprive a person of the ability to turn to the
courts for relief on the premise there was some material distinction.

[
150
] The critical factor in the present case is the nature and extent of
the personal interest of the owner in the validity of subsection 54(1)(b) of
the
Regulations
. This bears particular emphasis. The owner came by its
interest in stages, increment by increment. It started with nothing more than
the general interest of the public. But once it acquired a permit on the
combined authority of the
Act
and the
Regulations
, its interest
in the law, particularly in the law governing the conduct of permit holders,
became more specific. But even then, the owner's interest was no greater than
that of any other permit holder, and to that extent its interest remained
general, even abstract.  Once the owner was accused and found guilty of
violating section 54(1)(b) of
Regulations
, however, and faced an order
of suspension made against it in consequence, the nature of its interest in the
law underwent a significant change. At this stage, its interest became specific
and concrete, urgent even, because of the very real harm it was about to
experience at the hands of the Commission, acting upon the strength of this
regulation.

[
151
] In the light of this, the owner must be taken to have been in a
position to claim that the regulation was of no force or effect under section
52 of the
Constitution Act
on the footing the measure was inconsistent
with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
.
This, combined with the remaining
elements of the context in which section 2(b) of the
Charter
was raised,
served to allow the owner, as of right, to appear and be heard in relation to
the question under consideration. That is my view of the matter.

[
152
] I might add that, even if it were otherwise, the owner would still
have been able to appeal to the Court of Queen's bench for public interest
standing.

(c)     could the owner not have been accorded public

interest standing?

[
153
] Turning to standing on this basis, the Authority and the Attorney
General submitted in effect that such standing could not have been accorded the
owner, given the existing criteria governing the grant of public interest
standing and its application
in
Hy and Zel's Inc
. v.
Ontario
(Attorney General)
,
1993 CanLII 30 (SCC)
,
[1993] 3 S.C.R. 675
.

[
154
] As noted earlier, the Court of Queen's Bench enjoys the discretionary
power to grant persons standing to appear and be heard in relation to a
constitutional question where their interest in the question falls short of
entitling them to private interest standing. The exercise of this discretionary
power by the judges of the Court in a civil case is governed by three
requirements. The judge must be satisfied (a) that the proceedings raise a
serious legal question, (b) that the initiator of the proceedings has a genuine
interest in the determination of the question, and (c) that there exits no
other reasonable and effective way by which the question may come before the
court. (See
, for example,
Canadian Council of Churches
v.
Canada
,
1992 CanLII 116 (SCC)
,
[1992]
1 S.C.R. 236
).  Thus parties may be granted standing in a civil case, even
though they claim a violation not of their own rights or freedoms protected by
the
Charter
but only those of others, if the court is satisfied that
these requirements have been met.

[
155
] There was no suggestion on appeal that Mr. Justice Hrabinsky, had he
addressed the matter along these lines, would have erred in concluding that the
first of the criteria, going to merit and interest, were met. Indeed it was
conceded that these criteria were satisfied. Only the satisfaction of the third
was questioned. The issue, then, is whether it would have been open to him, in
the reasonable exercise of his discretion, to have treated the third of the
criteria as having been satisfied.

[
156
] It is clear on the face of the
Act
and the
Regulations
,
coupled with the stance of the Authority and the Attorney General, that the
constitutional validity of the impugned regulation is not going to come before
the courts at the behest of a permit holder charged with the offence of
violating the regulation. According to section 142 of the
Act
it is an
offence to contravene a regulation, but according to the Authority and the
Attorney General this does not apply to violations of the impugned regulation
by a permit holder, given the provisions of subsection 54(2) of the
Regulations,

which renders section 142 of the
Act
inapplicable to permit holders
who contravene subsection 54(1) of the
Regulations
.

[
157
] Nor is the constitutional validity of the impugned regulation going
to come before the courts at the instance of a performer charged with engaging
in entertainment of the nature of that prohibited by the regulation, for the
Act

creates no such offence. Nor does the
Act
otherwise regulate performers,
except indirectly by prohibiting permit holders from allowing them to engage in
entertainment of this sort.

[
158
] How else, then, might the constitutional validity of the impugned
portion of the regulation have been expected to be brought before the Court?
Without suggesting there was no conceivable way, I should not think it would
have been open to us on appeal to interfere, had Mr. Justice Hrabinsky taken up
this issue, concluded that this requirement had been met, and granted the
night-club owner status to appear and be heard in relation to the question of
whether the impugned portion of the regulation was inconsistent with
section
2(b)
of the
Charter
and hence of no force or effect under section 52 of
the
Constitution Act
.

[
159
] In other words, I believe it was open to Hrabinsky J. to find that
the requirements for public interest standing were met. While he did not do so,
since the matter had not been put to him, he might have done so, in which event
there could have been no quarrelling with the exercise by him of his
discretion, at least not in my opinion, having regard for the situation and the
applicable standard of appellate review. I might add that I can see nothing in
the decision of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Hy and Zel's Inc
.
to have
compelled him to turn down the owner's request to appear and be heard in
relation to the question under consideration.

[
160
] In sum, I cannot see how this Court could set aside the order under
appeal on the ground the owner of the night-club neither had, nor could have
been granted,
locus

standi
in the Court of Queen's Bench to
appear and be heard in relation to the question involving
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
.
In my judgment, then, the first ground of appeal must fail to the extent it
claims that the order under appeal falls to be set aside on the basis of
standing as such.

[
161
] That then brings up Mr. Justice Hrabinsky's determination of the

section 2
(b) issues, which is the subject of the second ground of appeal.

(2)
Section 2(b)
of the
Charter

[
162
] To the extent the impugned regulation bans "entertainment
containing a strip tease performance," the owner of the nightclub bore the
burden of establishing, along the lines laid down in
Irwin Toy,
that the
regulation was at odds with
section 2
(b). Accordingly, the owner had first to
establish that this provision was concerned with "expression," within
the meaning of
section 2
(b), and had then to establish that it restricted
freedom of expression in purpose or effect.

(a)

Whether the provision concerns "expression"

[
163
] The question is whether it does so to the extent it prohibits
entertainment consisting of a strip tease performance, since this alone is what
the order of the Commission was founded upon.  More precisely, then, the
question is this: Does entertainment consisting of "a strip tease
performance," within the meaning of subsection 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations,

constitute "expression," within the meaning of
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
?
The answer, of course, lies in the meaning and scope of each of these terms.

[
164
] As it appears in subsection 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations
, the
term "a striptease performance," used in conjunction with the term
"entertainment," is to be taken as meaning an act performed by a
performer before an audience of patrons, an act consisting of the piece by
piece removal by the performer of his or her clothing in a manner calculated to
arouse the desire of the audience to see progressively more, but without the
intention of completely satisfying that desire by the removal of clothing to
the point of nakedness. This is what the words "strip" and
"tease" suggest, both in themselves and in the light of the separate
treatment of "nude activity or entertainment" in subsection 54(1) (a)
of the
Regulations.
Consistent with their tantalizing object, such acts
traditionally feature background music and seductive dance, but do not entail
physical contact between the performer and any member of the audience. Hence
the term is to be taken to include an act featuring music and dance but to
exclude physical contact.

[
165
] It might be noted that this accords with the view taken by the Liquor
and Gaming Commission. In deciding that the performances of "The Men of
Extreme" were caught by 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations,
the Commission
impliedly construed the provision to this effect.

[
166
] The question, then, is whether such performances fall within the
scope of the term "expression." This term was construed
in
Irwin
Toy Ltd
. v.
Quebec (Attorney General)
as follows:

"Expression" has both a content and a form,
and the two can be inextricably connected. Activity is expressive if it
attempts to convey meaning. That meaning is its content. Freedom of expression
was entrenched in our Constitution...so as to ensure that everyone can manifest
their thoughts, opinions, beliefs, indeed all expressions of the heart and
mind, however unpopular, distasteful or contrary to the mainstream. [p. 968]

...

We cannot, then, exclude human activity from the scope
of guaranteed free expression on the basis of the content or meaning being
conveyed. Indeed, if the activity conveys or attempts to convey a meaning, it
has expressive content and
prima facie
falls within the scope of the
guarantee. Of course, while most human activity combines expressive and
physical elements, some human activity is purely physical and does not convey
or attempt to convey meaning....

The content of expression can be conveyed through an
infinite variety of forms of expression: for example, the written or spoken
word, the arts, and even physical gestures or acts. While the guarantee of free
expression protects all content of expression, certainly violence as a form of
expression receives no such protection. [p. 969-70]

[
167
] In the light of this, it is difficult to conceive of entertainment
consisting of "a strip tease performance" not falling within the
scope of the term "expression." Neither the Authority nor the
Attorney General, however, was prepared to concede the point, submitting that
such activity is purely physical and, as such, devoid of meaning.  With
respect, this is simply not so.  Were it so, there would be no material
distinction, for example, between persons removing their clothing in
preparation for going to bed and in the performance of a striptease act; the
one would be as expressively empty as the other. Moreover, the contention is at
odds with the decision of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
R.
v.
Butler
,

1992 CanLII 124 (SCC)
,
[1992] 1 S.C.R. 452
.  In that case, the Attorney General contended that
displaying acts of sexual intercourse in a pornographic movie, for instance,
could not be regarded as expressive because such acts are purely physical and
devoid of meaning. The court rejected that contention, holding otherwise.

[
168
] Certainly, the performances of "The Men of Extreme," which
provide concrete examples of the type of entertainment prohibited by this
provision, constituted a form of expression containing expressive content. The
elements of the performances--the musical selections, the costumes, the dances,
the doffing of the costumes, the highly developed physiques--offered a meld of
mood and image crafted to stimulate the imagination of the observer, as
undoubtedly it did, conveying a complex of ideas, sentiments, and emotions.

[
169
] As Mr. Justice Osler said of nude dancing in
Re Koumoudouros and
Metropolitan Toronto (City of)

(1984),
1984 CanLII 1858 (ON HCJ)
,
6 D.L.R. (4th) 523
at 526
[(Div.
Ct.):

[N]othing is more common in the artistic world than to
hear an individual express the desire to “make a statement”, and this may be by
means of the written or spoken word, the painted canvas, the etched stone, or a
print thereof, a musical composition, or an idea conveyed through the medium of
dance.  While the word burlesque may be thought by most to describe a form of
expression that is perhaps more vulgar than most of the artistic endeavours I
have mentioned, it is, nevertheless, a form of expression....

[
170
] Mr. Justice Cory voiced similar views in
Nordee Investment Ltd. v.
Burlington (City of)

(1984),
1984 CanLII 2037 (ON CA)
,
27 M.P.L.R. 214
at 219 (Ont. C.A.)
:

...It was argued that dancing cannot be a protected
form of expression, yet it would seem that dancing can express ideas and
emotions just as forcefully and artistically as do the written word, the
graphic arts, or music.  The lissome dancer has long been a symbol of grace and
beauty.  Whether one thinks of the performance of the chaste temple dancers of
Cambodia, Salome dancing before King Herod, or ballet companies and dance
troupes, they have all attempted to express ideas and to interpret or engender
emotions by means of the dance.  The fact that a dance is performed for profit
should not be a basis for the denial of the freedom granted by the
Charter
.
Artists through the ages have sought to make a wage or profit from their art.
No doubt, da Vinci and Michelangelo sought to profit from their paintings as
did Shakespeare from his plays.

[
171
] Were it not for the nature and setting of the strip tease performance
prohibited by subsection 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations
, such a performance
would be readily regarded, perhaps, as a form of "artistic
expression," which as
noted in
R.
v.
Butler
, at p. 486,
"rests at the heart of freedom of expression values."  These
performances, however, express something of an erotic sort, by means sure to
offend the sensibilities of some, and they occur far beyond the setting of the
traditional theatre, in establishments designed primarily to sell liquor. And
so many persons no doubt regard them as vulgar. For all that, however, and for
the fact as some will insist upon it that the appeal of such performances does
not extend beyond "the bar crowd," certainly not to "the theatre
set," they are no less artistic or expressive in nature.

[
172
] While their form and content may be regarded by many as base and
distasteful, the Supreme Court of Canada has repeatedly held that the content
of a statement, even if offensive, cannot deprive it of
section 2
(b)
protection.  As McLachlin J. pointed out
in
R
. v.
Keegstra
,

1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 S.C.R. 697
at 842
:

Attempts to confine the guarantee of free expression
only to content which is judged to possess redeeming value or to accord with
the accepted values strike at the very essence of the value of the freedom,
reducing the realm of protected discussion to that which is comfortable and
compatible with current conceptions.  If the guarantee of free expression is to
be meaningful, it must protect expression which challenges even the very basic
conceptions about our society.  A true commitment to freedom of expression
demands nothing less.

[
173
] In the light of all of this, and since the physical activity making
up the "strip tease performance" banned by the provision in issue
conveys or attempts to convey meaning, that activity may be seen to fall within
the scope of the term "expression." To this extent, then, the
judgment of Mr. Justice Hrabinsky cannot be said to be based in error.

(b)

Whether the provision restricts freedom of

expression in either purpose or effect.

[
174
] If its purpose, which is a function of the intent of the Lieutenant
Governor in Council at the time of enacting the provision, should lie in
restricting freedom of expression, then clearly the provision will be
inconsistent with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

[
175
] It may also be inconsistent with the section if the effect of the
provision, though not its purpose, should restrict freedom of expression. While
purpose and effect tend to coincide, they can diverge, as they are apt to do
when the effect of a provision is manifold and increasingly incidental. Where
only the effects of a provision are in question--the purpose being
unobjectionable--the matter has to be addressed on balance, with a view to
assessing the impact of the potentially offensive effects upon the lifeblood of
freedom of expression, which is to say upon the search for truth; the
participation in social and political decision-making; the pursuit of
self-fulfilment; and so on.

[
176
] The purpose must be assessed solely from the perspective of section
2(b), a point stressed in the majority judgment in
Irwin Toy:

When applying the purpose test to the guarantee of
free expression, one must beware of drifting to either of two extremes. On the
one hand, the greatest part of human activity has an expressive element and so
one might find, on an objective test, that an aspect of the government’s
purpose is virtually always to restrict expression.  On the other hand, the
government can almost always claim that its subjective purpose was to address some
real or purported social need, not to restrict expression.  To avoid both
extremes, the government’s purpose must be assessed from the standpoint of the
guarantee in question. [p. 973].

Turning from the
approach to the substance of the matter, the majority said this:

With regard to freedom of expression, if the
government has aimed to control attempts to convey a meaning either by directly
restricting the content of expression or by restricting a form of expression
tied to content, its purpose trenches upon the guarantee. Where, on the other
hand, it aims only to control the physical consequences of particular conduct,
its purpose does not trench upon the guarantee. In determining whether the
government's purpose aims simply at physical consequences, the question
becomes: does the mischief consist in the meaning of the activity or the
purported influence that meaning has on the behaviour of others, or does it
consist, rather, only in the direct physical result of the activity. [p. 976]

[
177
] Obviously the purpose of the provision in issue is to prohibit strip
tease performances in establishments permitted to sell and serve beverage
alcohol. Since such performances constitute a form of expression containing
expressive content, it is difficult to suppose the purpose does not lie, in one
way or another, in restricting freedom of expression.

[
178
] In this instance, the purpose of the law coincides with its effect,
an effect that is unmistakeable: All permit holders are prohibited from
allowing such form of expression; all performers are thus barred from engaging
in it; and all patrons are thus prevented from being exposed to it.  It is
impossible to suppose this is anything but the intended effect. And it is
difficult to separate the effect from the purpose. Indeed, the two are
inseparable.

[
179
] In this instance, too, the form and content of the expression are
inseparable. The one necessarily imports the other. The form conveys the
meaning, and to restrict the one is to restrict the other.

[
180
] In the light of all of this, the purpose of the impugned provision
must be taken to lie in limiting freedom of expression. If, in the words of
Irwin
Toy
, the Lieutenant Governor in Council did not aim in enacting this
provision "to control attempts to convey meaning...by directly restricting
the content of expression," it did so "by restricting a form of
expression tied to content."  And so "its purpose trenches upon the
guarantee."

[
181
] To the extent, therefore, that section 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations

bans "entertainment" consisting of "a strip tease
performance," it is to be taken as inconsistent with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
,
as Mr. Justice Hrabinsky held it to be.

[
182
] The second ground of appeal must therefore fail, bringing me to the
third ground, alleging error of law in the application of
section 1
of the
Charter
.

(3)
Section 1
of the
Charter

[
183
] The section reads thus:

1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such
reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free
and democratic society.

[
184
] It was with this in mind that Mr. Justice Hrabinsky concluded his
consideration of the
section 2
(b) issues with the observation: "It has not
been shown that s. 54(1)(b) of the Regulations can be demonstrably justified
under
section 1
of the
Charter
."  And it is this observation that
underlies the third ground of appeal, alleging he erred in "declaring that
section 54(1)(b) of the [
Regulations
] did not qualify as a reasonable
limitation upon the Respondent's freedom of expression for the purposes of
section 1 of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms."

[
185
] This scant mention of
section 1
by Hrabinsky J. does not provide much
of a foundation for this ground of appeal. Nor does it suggest, appearing as it
does in an otherwise thorough treatment of the constitutional issues to which
the case before him gave rise, that much if anything was made of this matter by
the Commission in its defence of the impugned regulation. Indeed this, too,
bears the marks of having being raised for the first time on appeal. Certainly
no evidence was adduced in support of a
section 1
defence of the validity of
the regulation. Nor was there any mention of this, either as a matter of fact
or law, in the written brief filed by the Commission in the Court of Queen's
Bench in advance of the hearing. The brief is confined, on this limb of the
constitutional attack upon the regulation, to arguing the
section 2
(b) issues
addressed by Mr. Justice Hrabinsky. Whether the oral argument on behalf of the
Commission extended beyond this is unclear, but in any event, and once again,
this makes for difficulty on appeal.

[
186
] Beginning with
R.
v.
Oakes
,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
,
[1986] 1 S.C.R. 103
, the
Supreme Court of Canada formulated a set of principles for the application of
the section, prescribing the criteria to be met in satisfying the requirements
of the section, identifying the party bearing the burden of establishing them,
and fixing the standard by which they fall to be established.

[
187
] Two central criteria must be met: First, the object of the limit must
be sufficiently important, in the sense it must at least relate to some
pressing and substantial societal concern, to warrant overriding a
constitutionally-protected right or freedom. Second, the means chosen to
achieve that object must be reasonable and demonstrably justified in proportion
to the importance of the object, and so the means must be carefully designed to
achieve the object and rationally connected to it; must impair as little as
possible the right or freedom in issue; and must, in effect, be proportionate
to the object.

[
188
] The burden of establishing these criteria rests upon the party
seeking to uphold the limit as reasonable and demonstrably justified. And they
fall to be established on the civil standard, namely on a balance or
preponderance of probabilities.  The standard is to be rigorously applied,

according to
R.
v.
Oakes
,
and convincing evidence will generally
required, "though there may be cases where certain elements of the
section
1
analysis are obvious or self evident."

[
189
] The Supreme Court picked up on this in deciding the freedom of
expression issues that arose in
Irwin Toy.
"It is now well
established," the majority stated, "that the onus of justifying the
limitation of a right or freedom rests with the party seeking to uphold the
limitation," and

where the basis for its legislation is not obvious,
the government must bring forward cogent and persuasive evidence demonstrating
that the provisions in issue are justified having regard to the constituent
elements of the s. 1...inquiry:
see
R.
v.
Oakes
, supra, at p.
138. In showing that the legislation pursues a pressing and substantial
objective, it is not open to the government to assert
post facto
a
purpose which did not animate the legislation in the first place (
see
R.

v.
Big M Drug Mart
, supra, at pp. 335): However, in proving that the
original objective remains pressing and substantial, the government surely can
and should draw upon the best evidence currently available. The same is true as
regards proof that the measure is proportional to the objective: (see
R.

v.
Edwards Books & Art Ltd
.
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R. 713
at p. 769)
. It is
equally possible that a purpose which was not demons trably pressing and
substantial becomes demonstrably pressing and substantial with the passing of
time and the changing of circumstances. [p.984]

[
190
] Consistent with all of this, then, the first line of inquiry into the
question under consideration has to do with the object of the impugned
provision and its importance. Given the connection between the object of an
enactment and its purpose, it is necessary to return to the purpose of the
provision.  In doing so, however, it must not be thought that the purpose is anything
but constant, a point made in
Irwin Toy
:

It is important, of course, to heed Dickson J.'s
warning against a "theory of shifting purpose" (
Big M Drug Mart
,
supra
, at p. 335): "Purpose is a function of the intent of those who
drafted and enacted the legislation at the time, and not of any shifting
variable." This is not to say the degree to which a purpose remains or
becomes pressing and substantial cannot change over time....But it is equally
true that the government cannot have had one purpose as concerns the division
of powers, a different purpose as concerns the guaranteed right or freedom, and
a different purpose again as concerns reasonable and justified limits to that
guarantee. Nevertheless, the same purpose can be assessed from different standpoints
when interpreting the division of powers, limitation of a guarantee, or
reasonable limits to that guarantee. [p.973-4].

[
191
] Obviously, the Lieutenant Governor in Council, acting on some
perceived societal concern, enacted the provision for the purpose of achieving
some object. The immediate object was to ban strip tease acts, a form of
expression conveying certain meanings, from being performed in establishments
permitted to serve alcohol-based beverages. But, of course, there was more to
the enactment of the provision than this, including the nature of the concern
and the ultimate object cabinet had in mind at the time. In other words, to
what end did cabinet act?  This must be identified. And once identified, the
importance of that end must be assessed in terms of whether it related to a
pressing and substantial societal concern. These are the issues to which the
first of the criteria governing justification of the provision under
section 1

gives rise.

[
192
] Although the Commission bore the onus of establishing these and the
other elements of the case for justification, it adduced no evidence of any
kind in the Court of Queen's Bench.  It did not even adduce any evidence of the
"legislative facts" of the matter--those going to the purpose and
background of the regulation in issue, including its cultural, moral, social,
or economic context:
Danson
v.
Ontario (Attorney General)
,
1990 CanLII 93 (SCC)
,
[1990]
2 S.C.R. 1086
at 1099
.  Nor did the Commission adduce any "social
science" or other evidence that might have shed some light upon these
issues.

[
193
] Since the provision amounts to subordinate legislation, and since
cabinet, unlike the legislature, functions in secrecy, the Commission might
have had some difficulty adducing evidence of this nature, especially evidence
of the legislative facts.  There seems no reason, however, to suppose that the
Authority, which would have had a hand in developing the regulations under this

Act
, or the Attorney General, who would have been involved in their
enactment, might have had any such difficulty.  But, of course, the Commission,
rather than the Authority, carried the case for justification in the first
instance, and the Attorney General chose not to appear and take part in the
proceedings in the Court of Queen's Bench.  This is not to criticise the
actions of either the Authority or the Attorney General, but only to comment
upon the difficulty in these circumstances of coming to grips with the issues
under consideration.

[
194
] The difficulty, of course, flows from the fact that, while
"certain of the elements of the section 1 analysis," in the words of
Oakes
,
may be "obvious or self evident," the whole of the matter must be
shown to be so if this ground of appeal is to succeed.

[
195
] It is easy to see that cabinet, in enacting clauses (a) and (b) of
subsection 54(1) of the
Regulations
, was intent on prohibiting erotic
entertainment in establishments serving alcohol--entertainment featuring
nudity, strip tease, and wet clothing contests provided in conjunction with the
consumption of alcohol. Identifying why it was intent on doing so is not so
easy.  Was it reflecting some cultural concern?  Perhaps, but only in small
measure, judging from the general political and cultural climate of the
Province.  Was it acting on some moral concern?  This is more likely, to be
sure, for these subjects are notorious for stirring up moral controversy in
some quarters of the Province. Or was it addressing some social concern,  a
concern, for example, with the effects of erotic entertainment and alcohol
consumption upon the attitudes and behaviours of members of the audience, or
with the effects of such entertainment upon the performers, or both?  This,
too, is more likely, given some of the political and social thinking abroad in
the Province. Or was cabinet apt to be reflecting a mix of some such concerns
and others?  More importantly, perhaps, what was the harm with which the
government was concerned, assuming the provision was harm driven?

[
196
] Since nude dancing and strip tease performances are tolerated in
establishments that do not serve alcoholic-based beverages, the provision seems
to be driven in the main by concern with the potential effects upon the
behaviour of persons being exposed to such forms of entertainment while
consuming alcohol, a concern for the conduct inspired by this combination of
erotic suggestion and alcohol consumption.  While not entirely clear, perhaps,
this much might be inferred, but beyond this the matter becomes increasingly
speculative.

[
197
] Counsel for the Liquor and Gaming Authority contended that the
provision was driven by "the many harmful results from the consumption of
alcohol," including crime, family violence, and society's perception of
women, saying that in the result "there is a legitimate legislative objective...in
dissociating stripping from the consumption of alcohol."  Assuming this
meant the provision was enacted out of concern for "the association
between alcohol consumption and violence against women," counsel for the
Attorney General agreed, saying the prohibition against erotic dancing while
beverage alcohol is being served was designed to further the object of curbing
violence against women. Either that, or of curbing this manner of degradation
or exploitation of women.

[
198
] While there may be something to these submissions, they want for a
proper foundation. There is nothing to establish the necessary nexus between
the key elements of these propositions, and so the argument cannot be acted
upon. This is especially so in light of the burden that lay upon the Commission
to establish its case for justification under section 1 of the
Charter--
the
burden, in the words of the majority decision in
Irwin Toy
, of bringing
forward "cogent and persuasive evidence demonstrating that the provisions
in issue are justified..."

[
199
] It might be noted, in illustration of the point, that counsel for the
Attorney General argued that the provision was enacted out of concern for the
degradation of women, for this type of activity portrays a pornographic-like
image of women "as sexual play things, hysterically and instantly
responsive to male sexual demands," according to a description of this
image referred to
in
R.
v.
Butler
,
and who "worship male
genitals" and judge themselves with reference to "the quality of
their genitals and breasts."  Some might agree with this. Others would
dispute it.  Few, however, would regard it as obvious or self-evident.

[
200
] While it is true that not every case entailing a constitutional
challenge based upon the
Charter
necessarily calls for evidence
establishing a factual basis for taking the measure of an enactment in light of

section 1
of the
Charter
, such cases are "exceptional" and
remain rare:
Manitoba (Attorney General)
v.
Metropolitan Stores Ltd.,

1987 CanLII 79 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 110
at 133
.

[
201

4.
Conclusion

[
202
] For these reasons, then, I am satisfied (i) that the night-club owner
established that subsection 54(1)(b) of the
Regulations,
to the extent
it prohibits "entertainment" consisting of "a striptease
performance," is concerned with and limits freedom of expression; (ii)
that the Commission failed in this instance to establish sufficient
justification for the limit under
section 1
of the
Charter
; (iii) that
in the absence of such justification, and for the purposes of this case, this
portion of the impugned regulation was properly taken on the face of it to be
inconsistent with
section 2(b)
of the
Charter
and therefore of no force
or effect under
section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
; and (iv)
that the Commission was thus shown to have lacked the power in this instance to
order the suspension of the owner's liquor permit for the reason it did. And so
I am satisfied that there is no tenable basis for this Court to interfere with
the exercise by Mr. Justice Hrabinsky of his discretionary power to make an
order in the nature of
certiorari
quashing the suspension by the
Commission of the owner's liquor permit. And so I would dismiss the appeal,
with costs to be taxed in the usual way.
